utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, you are continuing?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Can I turn to the question posed by the Court yesterday? In our submission, the Prosecution would have no right of appeal if the tables were reversed and the Crown had been frustrated in their attempt to present the evidence before the Trial Chamber. In our submission, that is for two reasons. First, the principle of equality of arms is intended in an ordinary trial to ensure that the Defence has the means to prepare and present its case equal to those available to the Prosecution which has all the advantages of the State on its side. We would commend to the Appeals Chamber the analysis of the relevant law by Judge Vohrah in the Trial Chamber in the judgement given on the 27th of November, 1996 on the Prosecution application for the disclosure of witness statements. His analysis begins at page 4 of that judgement, and he there says that he comes to the Prosecution's argument that the principle of equality of arms operates in this case to enable the Prosecution to have access to prior statements by the Defence witnesses. He goes on to say: "It is clear from the authorities submitted that the principle of equality of arms is inherent in the notion of a fair trial which is prescribed by international conventions. The principle is intended in an ordinary trial to ensure that the Defence has means to prepare and present its case equal to those available to the Prosecution which has all the advantages of the State on its side." He then sets out a number of authorities and continues towards the bottom of the page: "An even clearer statement in this regard was made by the European Commission of Human Rights when it stated," and the quotation reads that it "'is of the opinion that what is generally called 'the equality of arms,' that is the procedural equality of the accused with the public prosecutor, is an inherent element of a 'fair trial.'" A quotation of Pataki versus Austria is set out there in the judgement. He continues to review the relevant case law and then on page 5 of his judgement says: "This proposition that the equality of arms principle was intended to elevate the Defence to the level of the Prosecution, as much as possible, in its ability to prepare and present its case is evident in the case law arising out of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms 1950 and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 1966, both of which incorporate the principle of equality of arms in the concept of a fair trial." The concept of equality of arms is really a species of the principle that the defendant is entitled to a fair trial. If I could approach the question posed by the bench in a slightly different way and address the question of why this apparent imbalance exists in an area of law that embraces the word "equality" and why the Prosecution should not be entitled to what some may perceive to be the same advantages, the reason, in our submission, is that the principle of equality of arms is part of the defendant's right to a fair trial. The Prosecution have no right to a fair trial. They are not on trial. The burden of proof rests on the Prosecution. They have the task of discharging that burden, and in the trial process, the defendant is entitled to a fair trial. Unlike the Defence, the Prosecution can select when to issue an arrest warrant, and the trial process begins only when they are ready and have made the decision to proceed. They can delay, in reality, indefinitely until they are satisfied that they have a prima facie case. The trial process is then designed to examine that prima facie case and test it to see whether they have discharged the burden that the law places on them to prove the guilt of the accused. A warrant cannot be issued until evidence exists, and the trial process, in our submission, is designed to see whether that evidence that they have chosen to proceed to trial on can prove guilt. In contradiction, the Defence have no say over when proceedings are instituted by way of warrant, and thereafter, while they can have limited influence on the further progress of the trial, the two pressures of an unconvicted man in custody and the real anxiety of the court to achieve a trial within a sensible time frame combine to constrict the area of movement available to the Defence. It is for those reasons that we would submit that the principle of equality of arms, being part of the overriding principle that the defendant is entitled to a fair trial, is something that only, in reality, impacts on the Defence and not on the Prosecution. Before moving to the third ground of appeal, could I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, would it be convenient if, before you moved to the third ground, and I understand that the second ground does not now fall for consideration, for me to say a word on what you have just said? You would first of all appreciate that I was asking a question and not making a statement. The Court at this time has no position on these matters. The Court's interest is merely to test the limits of a theory which you are offering. Doubtless, we will hear in due course from the Prosecution about that part of your presentation in which I think you said something to the effect that the Prosecution has no right to a fair trial. Maybe at the appropriate time, the Prosecution would want to deal with the question whether the Prosecution represents the public interests at large and whether the public interests itself dictates a need that the Prosecution should also be entitled to a fair trial, the concept applying to both sides. May I draw to your attention a document which you may find useful but which perhaps does not form part of the record? It is a letter which Judge Cassese, who has drawn it to my attention, wrote on 19 September, 1996. He was then President of the Tribunal, and a letter was written to Mrs. Plavcic, acting president of Republika Srpska. I would have it shared around in a moment, and if there is no objection from any side, we could have it included in the record so that it forms part of the dossier. Mr. Registrar, would you hand it out? It's a letter in which President Cassese recalled that the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II, Judge McDonald, had brought something to his attention, namely, that there was a threat by the chief of security for the Prijedor area concerning the possible attendance of three witnesses who had been summoned by the Defence, and President Cassese was asking for the intervention of Mrs. Plavcic to ensure that those threats were not carried out. So that tends to support some of what you have been saying, and, incidentally, it also shows President Cassese and Judge McDonald did everything in their power to ensure that witnesses needed by the Defence would be available. Perhaps you would like to look at the letter and to make any use of it as you see fit, and the Prosecution also would like, I'm sure, to reply on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour. We would like to rely on the contents of the letter from President Cassese. It's a clear reflection of the ongoing frustration that Mr. Wladimiroff experienced during the course of the trial which, of course, was expressed and acknowledged by the judgement of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 530 in their judgement when they said: "A difficulty encountered by both parties has been their limited access to evidence in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, due in no small part to the unwillingness of the authorities of the Republika Srpska to cooperate with the International Tribunal. While witnesses called by the Prosecution, mainly Muslims and former residents of Bosnia, were now living in Western Europe or North American countries, most Defence witnesses, almost all Serb, were still resident in Republika Srpska." The judgement goes on to identify the steps taken by the Tribunal to assist the parties in attempting to alleviate the difficulties experienced by both sides but concluded at the bottom of paragraph 531 by saying in terms: "These steps did appear to alleviate the inherent difficulties of the situation," and, of course, the English word "alleviate" reflects a reduction of the problem or the difficulties, not the resolution of the problem. So it is perfectly clear that in the judgement of the Trial Chamber, they acknowledged and accepted that the inherent difficulties existed throughout the trial, and despite all efforts made by the Tribunal to overcome the difficulties placed in the path of the Defence by Republika Srpska, those difficulties still remained. It is a reflection of the ongoing problem addressed by Mr. Wladimiroff when he opened the case passage I didn't refer to yesterday where he said to the Court: "In preparing the Defence, we have struggled with the hostility and suspicion with which this Tribunal is viewed in Republika Srpska and in particular, in the Prijedor area. Those in power in this area have blocked avenues of investigation not only to the Prosecution but also to the Defence." So that is the problem that we are addressing. If I could just revert to the question of whether the Prosecution have a right to a fair trial. I don't want it to be thought that I am suggesting that the Prosecution have no rights. Of course, in the conduct of the trial, the Prosecution have many rights which, combined with the rights of the defendant, will ensure that a fair trial takes place: They have the right to call and present admissible evidence; they have the right, of course, to cross-examine and test evidence called by the Defence. In any trial process, and the trial process before the International Tribunal is no exception, there is always a balance between the conflicting parties, the balance being held by the judge or judges concerned to ensure that there is a fair trial. But it is a trial of the defendant at all times because he is the person who is on trial, and that is why the expression "the right to a fair trial" is always expressed as his right to a fair trial because it is his trial that everybody is engaged in, both Prosecution and Defence. I am not suggesting that the Prosecution have no rights in the trial process. Of course they do. And the rights that they have must be compatible with the fair trial of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I just want to understand you. Do I understand you correctly to mean this: The Prosecution has a right to participate in the trial and to ensure that the trial is fair, but if there is any unfairness in the trial, with particular reference to the matter of equality of arms, the Prosecution may not appeal; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: They cannot, in our submission, appeal if -- the question the Court poses presupposes that there is an unfairness if there is a lack of equality of arms vis-à-vis the Prosecution. I would put it slightly differently. I would say that if the Prosecution elect to proceed to trial against an accused person on a body of evidence and have determined that that body of evidence establishes a clear prima facie case upon which they can prove his guilt on a number of charges, then if they present that evidence before a Tribunal, there is no unfairness if other evidence exists which might add to or enhance the evidence upon which they have decided to proceed. I would venture to suggest that in almost every criminal trial in every jurisdiction in the world, there will always be more evidence that the Prosecution could find if given an unlimited budget to find it. There will always be other witnesses that could be traced, if unlimited manpower were devoted, other tests or examinations that could be made of exhibits if there was an unlimited budget to do so. The Prosecution have the control of the bringing of the case entrusted to them by either the state or, here, the International Tribunal. They make a decision that there is here a body of evidence that they have decided will prove those charges, and they say, "We don't need any more evidence. We can prove it on this evidence. There is no point going on for another year looking for another year of evidence or another two years and finding two more years of evidence. We are satisfied that we can prove these charges on this evidence, and therefore, we will issue a warrant and we will proceed to trial." They say to the Defence, "That is the evidence that we say proves you're guilty," and the Defence have the duty then to meet that evidence. Now, if that evidence that the Prosecution presents doesn't prove their case, doesn't get them home, then, in our submission, there is no unfairness for the Prosecution to say thereafter, "Well, we couldn't prove it. We'll go out and find some more evidence now, come to the Appeals Chamber, and present more evidence" in order to try to prove that which they couldn't prove in the first place. That, in our submission, ought not to be described as a lack of equality of arms; that, when properly analysed, is allowing the Prosecution what an English expression is, "two bites of the cherry." In other words, they are having a second chance at seeking to prove the case that they are, in reality, recognising the frailty of the case they originally presented which couldn't prove the charge and are seeking to shore up or make good the deficiencies in the case they presented for trial. So, in our submission, it is not accurately described as an absence of equality of arms, and to use that expression to describe the position of the Prosecution seeking to supplement their case by further evidence at this stage, is, in my respectful submission, a misuse of the way that phrase has been used and adapted by the courts in both the national and international jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say, Mr. Clegg, that any useful distinction can be drawn between the position of the Prosecution in a municipal system and the position of the Prosecution within the system promulgated by the Statute having regard to the peculiar realities on the ground? Does the Prosecution have available to it, within the context in which it is operating, the same superabundance of facilities which it may be expected to enjoy in the context of municipal arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, I am not privy to the budget, the financial budget, of the Prosecution, but it would seem, looking at the row of distinguished lawyers opposite me, that they aren't entirely devoid of financial support. They also, of course, have skilled and experienced investigators at their disposal. There is obviously a distinction, but in a municipal situation as well as an international situation, many witnesses do not willingly cooperate with the Prosecution. In the investigation of many crimes, witnesses will seek to avoid cooperating with the state, and that is something that is familiar in every domestic jurisdiction and, of course, is a feature of this jurisdiction. The trial process that has evolved before the International Tribunal is primarily an adversarial process, and if one concentrates on the principles of an adversarial process, it is my submission that the right to a fair trial cannot be legitimately extended to embrace a right for the Prosecution to call evidence in an appellate situation to remedy deficiencies in evidence that were exposed at trial. The reality would be that in every case where there was a verdict of not guilty, the Prosecution would be able to restart the investigation, find fresh evidence, and to use the appellate process as a second Trial Chamber. My fundamental objection is that the principle of the right to a fair trial is something that is peculiarly the right of the person who is on trial and not the right of anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Bench understands you. Would it be convenient for you to pass to the third ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The third ground of appeal is one that is limited to one decision of fact made by the Trial Chamber which concluded that it was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was guilty of the murder of two Muslim policemen, Osman Didovic and Edin Besic. That decision depended solely on the evidence of one witness, Nihad Seferovic. In our submission, the evidence of that witness was implausible when analysed and has been described by distinguished commentators as "curious." The background to his evidence is that he was a Muslim living in the area that had been under attack by Serb paramilitary forces. There had been a bombardment of the town where he lived, and he had fled to some nearby hills or mountains for safety. The cornerstone of his evidence was that before the bombardment, he had kept tame pigeons, and he was so concerned about their welfare that when the Serb paramilitaries were still in the town, he decided to return to the town in order to feed his pet birds. As a rational decision, that is, on any view, curious, because he was placing himself in the gravest of jeopardy in order to do no more than feed some pet birds who would have been most unlikely to have survived the bombardment of the town in any event; but that was the only explanation for him being in the town at the moment that these two men were killed, the evidence that he gave being that he approached the killing in an orchard to the distance of some 30 metres and, at that distance, was able to identify the defendant as the man who took two men out of a line of five and killed them in the area immediately in front of the Orthodox church. The evidence was identified in the judgement of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 393, and it merely recounts there the evidence that the witness gave; and at 394, it sets out the case for the Defence, that he was not in the town at the time those two people were killed. It was not, with respect to the Trial Chamber, the most critical analysis of the evidence of the witness Seferovic; it was, in truth, no more than a recitation of the effect of what he said. The evidence has been the subject of consideration and analysis by commentators, and if I could draw the Court's attention to just one, and it is the seventeenth divider of the Defence bundle of authorities, commentary on International Decisions by Michael Scharf of the New England School of Law, who says -- the article beginning on page 718 -- at page 719: "The most important Prosecution victory was the trial chamber's determination that Tadic had stabbed and cut the throats of two Muslim policemen outside a church after they were taken into custody by a group of Serb paramilitary forces. This is the only killing for which Tadic was found guilty by the trial chamber and was the key reason he received a twenty-year sentence. The finding is curious for two reasons." I underline the word "curious." "First, the only evidence to support it was the testimony of a single witness Nihad Seferovic, a Muslim who told the Tribunal the unlikely story that he had witnessed the murders when he had turned to Kozarac to feed his pet pigeons after the Serb take-over of the town. Second, nowhere in the indictment, which was amended twice by the prosecutor before trial, is there any reference to this murder. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber stated the murder was relevant because the list of acts alleged in the general persecution charge is preceded by the word 'included'." I take no point on the drafting criticism. It is the evidential position that we say should exercise the minds of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Scharf say that the witness told an "unlikely story"? Did he give any reasons to make out that proposition, that the witness told an "unlikely story"? Perhaps he did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The words "unlikely story" are followed by the assertion that the witness had returned to Kozarac to feed his pet pigeons after the Serb take-over, and I think that, as I read the commentary of Mr. Scharf, is what he was saying was unlikely because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was that the basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- on which he said that the witness's story was "unlikely"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes, on my reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: And the unlikelihood is obviously a reflection of the inherent improbability of anybody with any regard to their own safety willingly entering a town currently occupied by Serb paramilitaries when they were in the process of actively deporting the Muslims to concentration camps in order to feed a pet bird. It is, we would submit, such an unlikely and improbable story that any Tribunal would want to reflect on whether it could possibly be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: We would submit that of all the evidence before the Trial Chamber in relation to the various charges of which the appellant was found guilty, this was undoubtedly the weakest, and we submit that the Trial Chamber ought not to have relied upon it in order to convict the appellant of these two, effectively, two charges of murder. We say that for two reasons. First, we say that the unlikely account given by the witness is one that the Appeals Chamber is entitled to reflect on and to ask themselves whether there is not here a real danger that there has been a miscarriage of justice in relation to this charge. The accounted evidence of this witness is just so implausible, curious, unlikely, that to say that you could be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that what this witness said was true is, in our submission, a perverse conclusion for the Trial Chamber to have come to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How would you present this aspect of your case within the framework of the Rules which regulate and delineate the extent to which an appellate court can differ from findings of fact made by the trial court?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: So far as their approach to this witness is concerned, in our submission, the Trial Chamber misdirected itself as to the state of the evidence and an important respect that has significant impact upon this count. The position is that another witness called Dragan Opijak -- Opacic, referred to initially much more easily as "L," was a witness who, upon investigation, it was acknowledged that he was untruthful. In other words, there's no doubt this man was lying to the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber dealt with his evidence at paragraphs 553 and 554 of their judgement, and it's an important section. What they said was: "During the course of this trial the truthfulness of the testimony of one witness, Dragan Opacic, first referred to as Witness L, was attacked and ultimately, on investigation, the Prosecution disclaimed reliance upon that witness's evidence. The Defence contends that this incident is but one instance of a quite general failure by the Prosecution to test adequately the truthfulness of the evidence to be presented against the accused, instead of simply accepting as true the evidence given against a single Serb accused by a whole array of Muslim witnesses. "Two points should be made in regard to this submission. First, the provenance of Dragan Opacic was quite special. Apparently, of all the witnesses, he was the only one who came to the notice of the Prosecution as proffered as a witness by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in whose custody he then was. The circumstances surrounding his testimony were, accordingly, unique to him; the fact that his evidence came to be acknowledged as untruthful casts no light on the evidence of other Prosecution witnesses, none of whom share his provenance." Well, the fact was that the Trial Chamber had overlooked the fact that this crucial witness Nihad Seferovic, in fact, did share the same provenance as the witness whose evidence was acknowledged as being untruthful shared. It's our submission that where the Trial Chamber can be demonstrated to have misdirected itself as to what the evidence is, then that is a matter that the Appeals Chamber is entitled to rely upon when reviewing the decision in relation to this count. I'm not suggesting that a Trial Chamber could never convict anybody on the evidence of one witness. I'm not suggesting that for a moment. Clearly, in appropriate circumstances, one can have a safe verdict of guilty even if there is only one witness against an accused person, and I'm not suggesting that you can't. What I am suggesting here is we start off with a very unlikely and implausible account that has been the subject of critical analysis by independent commentators, and then one has built onto it a failure of the Trial Chamber to recognise something that they were clearly alert to and concerned about, namely, the fact of whether any Prosecution witness shared the provenance of the witness who was, in reality, planted in the trial in order to deceive the Court. That was the only sensible conclusion that could be made in relation to that witness, his evidence having been acknowledged as untruthful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right in my recollection that somewhere the Prosecution is averring that they supplied the Defence with a copy of the statement of this witness and that in that statement, there was a reference to the fact that the witness had been in touch with (redacted)? If so, did the Defence make any point of that fact in the course of the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think the position is this: The copy supplied by the Prosecution was in Serbo-Croat, and my understanding is that it was not translated at the material time, and it is only afterwards that the English version has been recognised as having a reference to the (redacted). I invite correction if I have misunderstood the position, but that is my understanding of it without having the opportunity for full research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thought you might find it convenient to deal with that aspect in the course of this branch of your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. It's also right, I think, that at the trial, the Defence were trying to exploit the position of Opacic in a much wider way than the Trial Chamber were prepared to entertain, and they were seeking to exploit it in order to cast doubt upon a wide raft of evidence that the Prosecution were relying on. What I am seeking to do is to very much narrow down the impact of that evidence in light, of course, of the judgement of the Court which reflects a concern as to the provenance of the witness, which was not a concern that would have been expressed until after the trial was over. So it's with the advantage of a sight of the judgement that I'm able to make the point that I make today to the Appeals Chamber. The position so far as the statement is concerned of this witness, which is annexed to the appellant's brief, is that in the second paragraph, he says: "Recently I had contact with persons in the (redacted) at which time it was determined that I may have knowledge of certain information ..." and as a consequence, he's put in contact with the International War Crimes Tribunal here in The Hague. Now, the effect of that is that this crucial witness, Seferovic, in fact approached the Prosecution from exactly the same provenance as the witness Opacic. Both were effectively offered to the Prosecution by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia, and in our submission, on any fair reading of paragraphs 553 and 554 of the judgement, any such witness is one that the Trial Chamber expressed a view that they would be concerned about, because it's the absence of a shared provenance that gives them comfort in relying upon the other witnesses. It must follow from that that the existence of a shared provenance will remove the comfort that otherwise existed. Now, it's perfectly clear here that the Trial Chamber firstly were concerned about a shared provenance and, secondly, relied upon the absence of it to accept the other civilian witnesses in the case. There is no recognition by the Trial Chamber of the important fact that this one crucial witness, the only witness on this count of murder, happened to come from the same government. They couldn't have known it. I understand that the statement, although exhibited as Defence Exhibit 14, I think, was exhibited, as I've said, in Serbo-Croat which nobody could read. The position is that a witness who has given an unlikely account, described as "curious" by distinguished commentators, being the only witness to a charge, in fact, shares a tainted source with another witness believed by the Prosecution to be perfectly honest, believed by everybody to be telling the truth, but who was subsequently accepted as being wholly untruthful. Indeed, the man, on the basis of the decision of the Trial Chamber, must have been committing perjury, must have been lying. They say it's accepted that his evidence was untruthful. That's only a courteous way of saying that somebody has lied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution disclaimed eventually any reliance on his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. It goes slightly further than that. They don't just disclaim reliance on it, which I presume one could do if one was merely concerned about the witness but not satisfied as to his untruthfulness, what they say in the next paragraph is: "His evidence came to be acknowledged as untruthful." So it goes further than just not relying on it. In our submission, a reflection on that evidence, a reflection on the link between the witness and the Government of Bosnia, a link that was not known or appreciated by the Trial Chamber, combines to raise a real doubt about the safety of the Trial Chamber's conclusion in relation to this charge. We would invite the Court, on reflection, to conclude that this verdict is unsafe and to quash the finding so far as it relates to those two counts of murder. Unless I can assist the Tribunal any further, those are our submissions on the third ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, let me see if my colleagues need your assistance any further. You may take your seat. Ms. Hollis, we have 20 minutes to go, I think. Mr. Clegg has done very well, indeed. He has exceeded expectations in that he has closed his argument 20 minutes before the scheduled time. Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution will attempt to follow that very fine example that has been set by the Defence. However, before we actually get into our argument, Your Honours, there are two matters that the Prosecution would request to deal with in private session having to do with redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You trust the Prosecution, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as of this morning, the argument --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let's be sure that the arrangements are in place. Go ahead, Ms. Hollis. No? No, not yet. Please proceed, Ms. Hollis. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The arrangements have been concluded. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, regarding the first ground of appeal of the Defence, before the Prosecution goes into its prepared remarks, I would first like to deal with the question that was raised by Judge Shahabuddeen yesterday regarding the application of this expanded principle of equality of arms and whether, using this expanded principle of equality of arms, if the Prosecution were denied evidence from a State that refused to cooperate or was obstructionist, if the Prosecution would have the same right of appeal based on that obstruction and failure to cooperate as the Defence would have using this expanded concept of equality of arms. First of all, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that, as the Defence conceded yesterday, this expanded definition goes beyond the accepted traditional concept of equality of arms, and we are urging in our submissions that the Court not take the invitation of the Defence to expand this concept but, rather, apply the traditional accepted concept of equality of arms. Under that condition, it would not be an issue of equality of arms. However, assuming for argument that equality of arms were to be expanded so that the situation the Defence is putting forth would impact equality of arms, we would suggest that you could not exclude the possibility that the Prosecution, in some circumstances, would have a similar right of appeal. We suggest that is true because the Prosecution is one of two parties to a trial. There is, of course, the accused, who has tremendous rights and tremendous protection. The other party, however, is the Prosecution who appears on behalf of the community whose laws are alleged to have been violated, and that community has a right to a fair trial, a fair hearing, about the alleged violation of those laws. So, indeed, the Prosecution, as representative of the community, does have a right to a fair trial. Secondly, Your Honours, if we look at the term itself, "equality of arms," the term itself implies parity; it does not imply that one side has all the rights and the other side has none of the rights. So the term itself implies that both sides would have equal rights. That would lead to the conclusion that under the appropriate circumstances, the Prosecution would also have the right to appeal. In addition, Your Honours, we are dealing with a situation, as put forth by the appellant, where all of the advantages the Prosecution is said to have in a national jurisdiction do not apply. It is a foreign state with whom the Prosecution is no more aligned than is the Defence that is obstructing, that is refusing to cooperate; and in this setting, in this International Tribunal, the Prosecution has no more link to that foreign state than does the Defence. The linkage that we have is through the powers conferred upon the Tribunal, and if the state does not cooperate with those powers, the Prosecution has no more ability to enforce that cooperation than does the Defence. The real issue of equality of arms would be if both sides have recourse to whatever measures are available to force cooperation. That would be the equality of arms that would be envisioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What do you say about Mr. Clegg's reference to something which was said in the Prosecution's brief to the effect that if, in fact, the material conditions indicated that a party was at a significant disadvantage, that would go to the question whether there was practical equality of arms even if there was full procedural equality? That is how I understood Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would suggest that that portion of our brief went beyond what we deemed to be equality of arms and spoke in terms of manifest injustice, and certainly we would agree that in national jurisdictions as well as international jurisdictions, there may be situations which arise which result in one party being deprived of justice, of a fair trial, because of the inability to obtain and present certain evidence. That has to be examined on a case-by-case basis. Our position is that it is not the case here and our position is that is not equality of arms. In our submission, we looked at what the Defence was arguing and said, "They're arguing equality of arms. We believe it is not an equality-of-arms issue, so what issues can they be raising?" The other issue that we talked about was abuse of process. We suggested that based on the submissions yesterday, where they agree the Prosecution in no way hindered their case, there is no abuse of process either. So we had three alternative arguments for ground number 1: The first was equality of arms, which we dismissed as not being applicable; the second was abuse of process, which we now know, based on the Defence concessions, is not applicable; and the third was this concept of a manifest injustice even if you had equality of arms in the traditional sense which is procedural equality before the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. During the Defence's presentation this morning, Judge Shahabuddeen also asked about a letter that had been submitted from then President Cassese to Mrs. Plavcic, and in that letter, the President expresses his concern that three named witnesses may not be allowed to appear in the trial. Indeed, we were aware of that letter, and all three of those witnesses named in that letter did appear and testify on behalf of the Defence in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does that destroy Mr. Clegg's point that there were, in fact, certain difficulties in procuring the attendance of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it does not. Further, Your Honour, we suggest that it is clear that there were difficulties; there were difficulties for both sides. Indeed, the Prosecution, if you will, had more equality in that sense than did -- the Defence had more equality than did the Prosecution because while the Defence, as I will discuss later, did obtain a measure of cooperation from the authorities of Republika Srpska, the Prosecution was never able to obtain a measure of cooperation from the officials of Republika Srpska. I would suggest to you, however, that that is not the test to be applied on this appeal. It is not whether they received full cooperation, it is not whether they achieved everything they wished to achieve. The question is: Looking at the ability they had to present a case and to cross-examine the Prosecution evidence, did this lack of full cooperation from Republika Srpska deny the accused a fair trial? We believe that the issue is somewhat different than the Defence has presented it. Your Honours, if I could turn to the prepared remarks to highlight the Prosecution position? Through the appellant's submissions yesterday, we submit that it is no longer a valid argument that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, may I suggest to you that if you are moving on to your prepared submissions, that perhaps we had better take the coffee break at this time? We can have half an hour and resume at twenty to eleven. Would that meet with your convenience?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then the court stands suspended for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, as the appellant has conceded, the traditional accepted concept of the principle of equality of arms has not been violated in this case; however, the Defence invites this Chamber to expand the traditional principle of equality of arms. The Prosecution submits to the Chamber that you should decline this invitation. The expansion that the Defence would have you make, we would suggest, is not consistent with the end that is sought to be achieved by the principle of equality of arms; that is, that before the courts that try cases, both parties would have parity. They would have equal access to the powers of the court to enable them to bring their case forward. Regarding this question of whether the equality of arms has been violated here and whether the traditional concept will be adhered to or an expanded view will be adopted, it is most important that the Appellate Chamber does speak to this and speak to it very clearly in order to ensure that Trial Chambers and practitioners before this Tribunal have the benefit of that guidance in defining what that concept means here in this Tribunal. We submit to you that when you look at the real basis of ground number 1, that the issue that presents itself is whether the degree of obstruction and lack of cooperation that was exhibited on the part of Republika Srpska denied the accused a trial that was fundamentally fair. There is some dispute, apparently, as to the test that should be applied to determine this issue. At one point in argument, the appellant seemed to point to this Appellate Chamber's decision on additional evidence in order to show what test should be applied. If you will recall, and I am paraphrasing, the appellant seemed to argue that the decision on additional evidence shows that there was relevant Defence evidence that was not called at the trial either because witnesses were intimidated or because a lack of full cooperation on the part of Republika Srpska denied the Defence the opportunity to discover the existence and location of these witnesses. The argument continued that had Republika Srpska cooperated fully, the Defence would have been able to call at least some of these witnesses as a matter of right. Republika Srpska did not fully cooperate, and as a result of that, the witnesses were not available at trial, so that now, on appeal, the appellant must show more than relevance in order to use the evidence that could be obtained from these witnesses. Therefore, the argument ran, Republika Srpska's conduct denied the appellant his trial right to call evidence based on relevance and imposed upon him a higher burden and thereby denied his right to a fair trial. The Prosecution submits that this argument does not set forth the test to be applied in evaluating ground number 1 and should not be adopted by this Chamber. To adopt the appellant's argument would mean that any time an accused was denied relevant evidence at trial, then on appeal, the appellate court must reverse the conviction, order a new trial, or take other drastic corrective action. It would mean that such a denial of evidence is per se reversible error. It would mean that Appeals Chambers, when faced with this issue, cannot assess the merits of the relevant evidence in determining if corrective action is required. We suggest that such an argument ignores the reality that it is not uncommon that relevant evidence will not be available at trial, it is not uncommon that such evidence becomes available after trial. The argument that has been put forward by the appellant ignores the fact that the right to a fair trial does not mean the right to a perfect trial and it does not mean the right to call all relevant evidence that the Defence may wish to call. We also suggest that the argument ignores the significant interest of society in the finality of judgments and it ignores the fine balance that criminal law strives to achieve between giving effect to the finality of judgments and the need to ensure a fair trial. That balance requires assessments of the merits of the alleged error, assessment of the impact of an error, if it does exist, on the integrity of the trial decision. The Prosecution suggest that the test to be applied in evaluating this ground of appeal is given to us by appellate practice and by the Tribunal's Statute and Rules, and that that test does rightfully include a showing by the moving party beyond relevance of evidence that was not presented at trial. It includes a showing of the impact of any error on the integrity of the trial. If the appellant is arguing that there is an error of law, the prejudice that must be shown, according to the Statute of this Tribunal, is that it was an error of law such that it invalidated the decision. If the appellant is basing his argument on an error of fact, it must be such an error of fact that occasions a miscarriage of justice. So you must have a relevant showing of error plus the appropriate level of prejudice before corrective action is required on appeal. The Statute and Rules of this Tribunal regarding the submission of additional evidence are consistent with these principles in that they require some showing beyond relevance before such additional evidence must be admitted and considered. If we look at this issue of ground 1 in this context, we suggest that rather than showing a denial of fair trial, the decision on the additional evidence is consistent with no denial of a fair trial. First of all, in regards to the impact of lack of cooperation by Republika Srpska, the majority of the additional evidence that was offered was found to have been available to the Defence at trial. Secondly, in regard to that portion of additional evidence which was found not to be available, the Appellate Chamber, after careful consideration, found that the interests of justice did not require that it be admitted for consideration at this date. Assessing the alleged error and the impact of that error, the Prosecution submits that this Chamber must look at this alleged error and its impact in the context of what evidence was adduced at trial both by the Defence and by the Prosecution. The Defence wanted to present an alibi case at trial and they also wanted to attack the identification of the accused. As for the alibi that they wanted to present, they knew the identity of many of the witnesses that they wanted, so they were not prevented from knowing the identity of witnesses that they wanted. Were there other witnesses that they wished they could have searched for? We do not argue that point. At trial, the Defence was able to put on a very vigorous defence. In terms of identification issues, they were able to call an expert who went into great length about identification, and they were very vigorous and very complete in their cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses regarding the issue of identification. In regard to alibi, they were able to call witnesses to attempt to establish an alibi. They were able to put on documentary evidence concerning this alibi. The Defence was able to do this at trial, in part, certainly because of the broad disclosure obligations that the Prosecution has, so that we have to give them evidence relating to our witnesses and exculpatory evidence, but the Defence was also able to do this at trial because they did receive a measure of cooperation from Republika Srpska. At trial, the Defence called 40 witnesses; 35 of those witnesses were from Republika Srpska; three of those witnesses were police who appeared with the authorisation of the authorities in Prijedor. They submitted documentary evidence to attempt to establish an alibi that they received from Republika Srpska predominantly from Prijedor, including police evidence of duty rosters and other such evidence relating to alibi. This some measure of cooperation began in advance of the trial. As early as 1995, the Defence was able to obtain some documentary information from Republika Srpska. As of February of 1996, the Defence was able to say that there were remaining obstacles, but they believed that the major obstacles had been removed. Some of the ways that they did this was to obtain a letter from Mr. Karadzic allowing them to investigate their case. To receive an undertaking from the Minister of Interior in Pale to allow them to undertake their case, they presented this letter from Dr. Karadzic to the chief of police in Prijedor and in February received written permission signed on behalf of the chief of police to investigate in the area of Prijedor, to talk to witnesses. Was this full cooperation? No, it was not. Was this grudgingly given? Yes, it was. But they did receive cooperation that allowed them to go forward with their theory of the case at trial. Yesterday, there was a question raised about whether this delay between the Prosecution case and the Defence case was the result of lack of cooperation from Republika Srpska. The answer to that, we submit, is "no." There was a three-week break between the Prosecution case and the Defence case. The break was at the Defence's request, and the reason for the break, according to the Defence, was to allow them to organise the bringing of their witnesses to the Tribunal to testify. Also, they did say there was some investigation they had left, but the main reason was to allow them to organise to bring their witnesses to the Tribunal to testify. If we look at the ability that the Defence had and showed to have at trial to bring evidence and we look at that in the context of a Trial Chamber that was very supportive of the Defence's efforts and very sensitive to their problems, we suggest that there is no basis to conclude that the Defence was denied a fair trial. In assessing this issue, we must, of course, look at what the Defence did at trial. It was mentioned yesterday that the Defence at no time during the trial requested a stay of proceedings, and it was discussed that this, in part, could have been because of a concern about further delaying the trial. However, looking at the record of trial, there is no evidence in the record to show that the Defence ever asked that the case be dismissed because of lack of cooperation. That was another option that they had. If they reached a point where they felt they could not get a fair trial, they could have requested a dismissal of the case and reopened that issue. They did not do so. By not doing so, they did not give the Trial Chamber the opportunity to take additional measures to try to overcome obstacles they were still facing. We would suggest that by not doing so, they gave you an indication that they did not believe their right to a fair trial had been violated. Recall, please, that there were four Defence attorneys who were working on behalf of the appellant at the trial, two very experienced criminal defence attorneys from The Netherlands and two experienced criminal defence attorneys from Great Britain. So we had both systems of criminal justice represented. Surely they would have known the measures available to them if they believed that they were being denied a fair trial. They did not exercise those measures, and we ask that this Appellate Chamber keep that fact in mind when they conclude if, indeed, a fair trial was denied. At the trial, the Trial Chamber had the benefit of this Defence evidence, it also had the benefit of very rigorous and vigorous cross-examination of the Prosecution's evidence, and it had available to it the Prosecution evidence itself. Based on all of that, the Trial Chamber made its conclusions about proof beyond reasonable doubt. It is in that context, we suggest, that the Appellate Chamber must look at the issue of whether the lack of full cooperation denied the appellant a fair trial. We suggest the Defence has not made the requisite showing that the lack of full cooperation was such that they were denied their ability to put on a case such as they wished to present. They were not denied the right to call witnesses. Would they want more? Yes. Is that the test? No. The lack of full cooperation did not result in invalidating the decision, the judgement in this case, nor did it occasion a miscarriage of justice. We suggest that this ground for appeal should be dismissed. Now, moving on to ground 3 of the appeal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I better look to my colleagues to see if they need your assistance any further on that point. Then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, before going into the prepared remarks, I would first like to deal with some of the issues that arose this morning in the Defence argument. The appellant seemed to argue that because this witness, Nihad Seferovic, would say that he would go into a town where the Serbs were taking it over to feed his birds, that his testimony is inherently incredible. Now, is this a decision many people would think is rational? Of course, it is not. But how many times have we heard stories of people going into burning buildings to rescue pets, of doing other things that subject them to a very real and immediate threat of death to save a pet? Are these rational acts? No, they're not. Are these acts that people do engage in? Yes, they are. The question really becomes, by virtue of this act, going to feed birds in a dangerous environment, is that explanation so implausible, so out of sync with the way human beings act, that that would render this witness's entire account unworthy of belief? In evaluating that, of course, we have to look at the entire testimony. We have to look at the fact that this witness was very, very strenuously, very comprehensively cross-examined, and the Trial Chamber had the benefit of that in arriving at its conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, would you help the bench by addressing us on this point: To what point does disbelief in the evidence of that witness have to reach before an appellate court could disagree with the assessment made by the trial court?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would submit to you that, of course, appellate judges may reverse findings of facts. That is inherent in the Statute; that's inherent in appellate practise. In doing so, however, great deference must be given to the Trial Chamber, three learned jurists who actually saw and heard this witness and all the evidence and had the ability of being there as it was delivered in making their assessment of credibility. It is ultimately an assessment of credibility that we are dealing with here. Taking that deference in mind, however, we would suggest that the standard to be applied is that this Appellate Chamber would overturn that determination if it were to conclude that no reasonable person could have concluded what the Trial Chamber concluded. It is not a matter of substituting another reasonable person's judgement. It is a matter of determining that no reasonable person could have concluded this. We would suggest that that is the standard that should be applied in this case, and we would suggest that applying that standard, that standard has not been met. An issue came up in the Defence argument about the statement of Mr. Seferovic. We would like to clarify what actually occurred at trial concerning that statement. First of all, the statement in question was a statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. That statement was taken down in English. The English version, which was the only version we had, the English version of that statement was provided to the Defence in 1995. The Defence had that translated into B/C/S so that the accused could read the statement. The Defence at trial used the B/C/S version to show the witness who could not read English. At trial, the Defence did not offer into evidence either the English version that they had been provided or the B/C/S version. At trial, the Defence did not bring up to the Trial Chamber the information in the statement about the witness's contact with the (redacted). The Defence was aware of that information. It had been provided to them in English. They did not bring it up. They did not bring it up in argument when they were discounting this witness's testimony in closing argument. We suggest to you that the Defence, in making their argument here, has misstated the Trial Chamber's findings regarding the witness Dragan Opacic, and we suggest to you that that misstatement has been used as a basis to build an argument that Nihad Seferovic is tainted because he is similarly situated to Dragan Opacic. The Trial Chamber stated that the circumstances surrounding the testimony of Dragan Opacic were unique, and they stated that "he was the only one who came to the notice of the Prosecution as proffered as a witness by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina in whose custody he then was." We put emphasis on those last words. That is what makes him unique. He had been captured as a soldier and was held and made statements, and we became aware of him through the Bosnian government. That is not the situation with Nihad Seferovic. In addition to that, much has been said about Witness L and what the Trial Chamber found or did not find and what the Prosecution did or did not do. Again, let us submit to you that the situation with Witness L was such that, at a point in the proceedings, the Prosecution became convinced that Witness L had lied about his family situation. That lie became very obvious. That is what we know he lied about. What else did he lie about? We don't know. But the Prosecution felt that because now his truthfulness was put at issue, we could not offer him as a witness who would be worthy of belief. Therefore, we withdrew him. We at no time said we believed he lied about Trnopolje. The point was we didn't know and we did not, because of his other lie, have sufficient confidence in him to put his version forward. It is interesting to note in that regard that the Defence found out about Dragan Opacic's family and that they were alive because they were able to go to Trnopolje. They knew his name. They knew what his position supposedly had been at the camp. They were asking around in the area, and someone told them they knew a Pero Opacic and where he worked and that Pero Opacic had been a guard in Trnopolje. Pero Opacic turned out to be Dragan Opacic's brother. So did Dragan Opacic have the opportunity to go there? Yes. But we could no longer be confident of his reliability, so we withdrew him. Because we withdrew him, there was no need to ever find that he committed perjury - that was not found - nor was he ever prosecuted for perjury. So the taint on this witness had to do with his lies about his family situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did the Court ask the Prosecution to investigate?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, and the Prosecution did investigate and gave its results, and the results that the Prosecution came up with do not support the Defence allegation that he had been planted by the Bosnian government. We were allowed full access to all information and were not able to draw that conclusion from our investigation. Now, going back to this situation at trial, trial Defence counsel knew of the circumstances surrounding Dragan Opacic, they knew about Nihad Seferovic, they knew about his statement; Defence counsel at trial never equated the two. Defence counsel at trial never asked that Nihad Seferovic be recalled after the situation with Dragan Opacic became obvious. Defence counsel at trial never asked that Nihad Seferovic's testimony be struck because he was tainted as was Dragan Opacic. Trial Defence counsel did none of those things. They did not argue the similarity in closing argument. Why is that? Because they concluded, the appropriate conclusion, that these two were not similarly situated. So that is not a basis for discounting the evidence of Nihad Seferovic. There is no need for corroboration of a witness. The Trial Chamber looked very carefully at this witness, concluded he was reliable. The Defence has made no showing that would require you to go behind the decision of the Trial Chamber and would require you to not give them the deference to which they should be entitled and we would ask that you also deny this ground of appeal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Let me see if there are any questions from colleagues. No. There are no questions. Thank you very much for finishing ahead of schedule. I see on my scheme here, Mr. Clegg, that you are down to reply for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Let's see if we can maintain the progress that we have hitherto. Dealing with the first ground of appeal, in our submission, the Appeals Chamber shouldn't be diverted by the description or labelling of the principle that lies behind this ground. It matters not whether one refers to it as "equality of arms" or "the defendant's right to a fair trial." It seems to be acknowledged by the Prosecution that if the effect of the obstruction were such as to deny the appellant a fair trial, then that is a factor that ought legitimately be reflected in a decision in his favour before this Tribunal. In our submission, it doesn't matter enormously whether you describe it as "equality of arms" or describe it as "a right to a fair trial" or describe it in the way that the Prosecution have in the course of their brief that I drew the Court's attention to during the submissions I made yesterday. It is the principle that underlines what we submit rather than the labelling. In our submission, the fact that there was obstruction is accepted and acknowledged. No one denies that such cooperation as was achieved was given grudgingly and normally under pressure applied from this Court or elsewhere. The final assessment must be whether the degree of obstruction was such that the appellant's right to a fair trial was prejudiced. In this regard, in our submission, it is irrelevant what lack of cooperation the Prosecution suffered. There is no concept here of a quid pro quo, that the obstruction of one side can be balanced against the obstruction of the other. One side in this process was in jeopardy of losing his liberty and was on trial; one side was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did Ms. Hollis quite put it that way, that obstructions suffered by one side could be balanced by obstructions suffered by the other side, or was she pointing to obstructions suffered by the Prosecution as indicative of her conception of the idea of equality of arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think it may well have been expressed in the way that has just been indicated. The effect of expressing it in that way, when analysed, is still, is it not, to offset the impact of obstruction to the Prosecution against the impact of obstruction to the Defence and asking the question, when looking at it in the round, has a fair trial still been possible? In our submission, it is not a question of weighing each side against each other. The inquiry ought to be focused on what we submit is the right of the accused to have a fair trial, and the question that, in our submission, ought to be addressed, is whether his right to have a fair trial, which must, in our submission, entail and embrace his right to present his case in a proper way before the Trial Chamber, whether that was frustrated or not; and if it was, we would submit that that does affect his fundamental right to a fair trial. We would express it in the terms of an extended principle of equality of arms, but that may, to some extent, be more a label than a principle. The issue for the Appeals Chamber, if I may respectfully suggest, is an assessment of the degree of obstruction as it impacted on the Defence, not as it impacted on the parties generally. We would submit that every element of obstruction would not result in an unfair trial. Obviously, if one take an extreme example, if one witness on one minor, peripheral issue was prevented from attending, nobody could sensibly argue that could prevent a fair trial. If one went to the other extreme and you could demonstrate that 35 crucial witnesses as to fact were all prevented from attending, then it may be very easy to say that the obstruction prevented a fair trial. Here, the element of obstruction that we can see in this case fell in the middle of those two extremes, and it is, we would submit, for the Appeals Chamber to resolve whether the level of obstruction, in fact, went so far as to deny this appellant a fair trial. In our submission, it did. It went beyond obstructing the periphery of the case but went to the obstruction of the Defence in putting forward matters that were central to the case they were presenting, and in those circumstances, we would submit that that level of obstruction was such as to deny the defendant a fair trial. If I may move to the third ground of appeal? I, of course, accept what Ms. Hollis has said so far as the history of the exhibit in the case which was referred to clearly as Defence Exhibit 14 but, as I understand, it did not become a formal documentary exhibit. It had some nebulous character between a full exhibit and something else. But the Serbo-Croat document did have a label attached to it, as I understand it, that referred to it as a Defence Exhibit even if it wasn't a form of document that was copied for the Court. The sequence, as I understand it, was that Seferovic gave evidence a considerable period of time before Opacic, and therefore, the importance of the link between Seferovic and the Bosnian government would have been quite unknown to anybody until the untruthfulness of Opacic was discovered during the course of his evidence. So it is important to remember the sequence of events. Whether one makes a decision to recall a witness for further cross-examination is always, of course, a difficult decision for an advocate to make. Sometimes the advocate may think that the witness's account, as it stands, is not one that the Trial Chamber would be likely to accept. They may make a value judgement, if one likes, and think that enough had been done so far as that witness's testimony is concerned. It may be -- I don't know what the reasoning, if any, was behind the Defence team at trial here. But that doesn't alter the fact that in an appellate jurisdiction reviewing a decision of fact, the Appeals Chamber is entitled to have regard to all relevant evidence and, in our submission, isn't constrained by what questions were asked in the lower court or the way that the case was necessarily left to the Trial Chamber. One's entitled to look at all the material that is legitimately before you and to ask the question whether this Court is satisfied that the decision of the Trial Chamber, in accepting the evidence of Nihad Seferovic, was the right decision or not. I don't disagree with the approach of Ms. Hollis as to the standard that the Appeals Chamber would need to address in approaching that. It is not a question of substituting your view of the witness for the view formed by the Trial Chamber who, of course, had the benefit of hearing the witness and hearing the cross-examination. In our submission, the standard is rightly expressed by Ms. Hollis. The standard is whether this Chamber can say that no reasonable person could conclude that the evidence of that witness was capable of proving beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was the person responsible for those deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You assert then that the Trial Chamber would not have been acting as a reasonable person if they accepted the testimony of Seferovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I do make that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I want to grasp your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes. I embrace that proposition with the added advantage of the concerns of independent commentators on the evidence and what we submit is a legitimate factor for this Chamber to take into account, namely, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, may I ask you this: You have referred to the commentator's reference to that aspect of the matter. Are you relying on the commentator's observations as some kind of authority in itself or are you adopting his remarks and making them your own?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The latter. The final matter so far as ground 3 is concerned is that we do submit that the failure of the Trial Chamber to recognise the common source of the evidence between Opacic and Seferovic is something that the Appeals Chamber is entitled to have regard to. The fact is that in dealing with the evidence of Opacic, the Trial Chamber expressly identified a link between that witness and the government of Bosnia. I mean, that is a fact, and it also concluded the witness was accepted as being untruthful, and it rejected a suggestion of contamination on the basis that it formed the view that the witness was the only one who had links with that government. Now, it is a remarkable coincidence but it is a fact that this other witness, who is the only one to this incident, also has the same links, and I do ask rhetorically whether the Trial Chamber had been alerted to that, and it may be that the connection was not something that had been drawn to their attention, indeed I accept it wasn't, it may be they hadn't got this statement in front of them in English to enable them to make the connection, but they were denied the connection, for whatever reason, and had they noted, I ask the question rhetorically, whether they would, in those circumstances, have accepted the evidence of Nihad Seferovic. Of course, one knows not the answer to that question. But I do say that that enables the Appeals Chamber, when approaching this very difficult issue, to take into account the fact that the Trial Chamber did not have one significant factor before them that you have the advantage of, namely, the knowledge that this witness shared a common source with the witness Opacic that the Trial Chamber took the view could be a tainted source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did the Defence make any representations to the trial court about the circumstance on which you rely, that the B/S/C statement of the witness was not accessible to counsel, or did the Defence try in some way to have a translation made of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I think the Defence must have had a translation, on reflection. I don't think there can be any doubt about it. Because when you read the evidence of Seferovic, part of the statement is put to him in cross-examination, so they must have had it in English. They clearly never drew the Trial Chamber's attention to the link that I am now making. In our submission, that does not preclude the Appeals Chamber, in reviewing the safety of a conviction, in looking at that material, and we would invite the Appeals Chamber to look at all of that material and then to ask oneself the question whether, in light of that link and in light of the inherent improbability of the account, whether one can say that no reasonable person could conclude safely and beyond reasonable doubt that that witness was giving an accurate account of seeing the appellant commit those two murders. We would invite the Appeals Chamber to approach the ground in that way. Unless I can assist you any further ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me turn to my colleagues. Please be seated, Mr. Clegg. I believe that concludes the arguments on appellant's appeal on judgement. We are now in a position to begin the second phase of our three-pronged exercise, and that is Prosecution's cross-appeal on judgement. I have forgotten, Ms. Hollis, who is handling this department for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are two of us, and Mr. William Fenrick will begin with the issues relating to international armed conflict and crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We are prepared to proceed up to 12.55 but we recognise, being not unmindful of the convenience of professionals, that you might find it more useful and appropriate to commence afresh when we resume at a quarter to three. If you wish to begin now, we are quite available to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we appreciate your courtesy, and we would request that we be allowed to begin our argument when we reconvene so that it is not interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. That is agreeable, is it? Then we stand adjourned until 14.45; is that it? Yes, a quarter to three. Thank you very much --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.23 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you ready, Mr. Fenrick?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May we signal to you at the start that you might usefully help us on two grounds, grounds 3 and 5, on this point: Ground 3, I think, concerns the definition of crimes against humanity, and the point there is whether the definition is broad enough to include acts committed for purely personal reasons. The second has to do with the question of the right of a party to disclosure of a witness statement after the witness has testified. We ask your assistance only for this reason: We observed that in your briefs I think you mention that nothing really turns upon these points so far as a reliefs prayed for are concerned. I think you put it on the basis that these are matters of general importance on which it would be desirable to have a pronouncement from the Court. We have no position on this matter, but it is an aspect of which we would be indebted to you for your assistance, both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish me to address that in the sequence as I'm addressing the other arguments or right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just as you please, Mr. Fenrick. We just thought that we would mention that to you at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honours, I will be speaking to grounds 1, 3, and 4 on behalf of the Prosecution in the cross-appeal, and I will address the specific issue that you referred to when I get to my discussion of ground 3. My colleague, Ms. Hollis, will be addressing grounds 2 and 5, and I'm sure that she will address the same issue when she gets to ground 5 in her submission. Our intention is that I will address grounds 1, 3, and 4 for approximately one and a half hours, although I would expect that the major portion of my presentation would, in fact, relate to ground 1, and then my colleague, Ms. Hollis, would like to have an hour of your time after I am finished to address the other grounds. If I may start with ground number 1, our appeal ground, of course, is the finding by the Trial Chamber that it had not been proved that the victims were protected persons under Article 2 of the Statute. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that it had not been proved that the victims referred to in various counts charging the appellant under Article 2 of the Statute with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 were protected persons under the provisions of the relevant convention. As a consequence of this finding, the accused was acquitted on counts 8, 9, 12, 15, 21, and 32. This finding was also part of the reason for the acquittal on count 29. A major reason for the erroneous decision on protected persons was the preceding, we submit, erroneous decision by the majority of the Trial Chamber to rely exclusively upon the effective control test that it derived from the judgement of the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case in order to determine the applicability of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions. The Prosecution submits that the Nicaragua case was concerned with state responsibility, not with individual criminal responsibility. Further, in the case, the ICJ deliberately avoided deciding which body of treaty rules applied by focusing on what it referred to as the minimum yardstick of the rules contained in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 which, in the view of that court, applied to all conflicts. Further, it is our submission that the Nicaragua case would be relevant after a fashion if what we were concerned with here was a situation where, in fact, there was no other indicator of an international armed conflict existing within Bosnia. If there was no proof of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia troops being engaged in combat in 1992, it is possible that the Nicaragua decision would be of some relevance in connection with determining whether or not Yugoslavia was engaged in an international armed conflict through its direct control of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. But as that, in fact, is something which is not at issue, the Trial Chamber has already accepted that Federal Republic of Yugoslavia troops were involved in the conflict after the 19th of May, 1992, we submit the Nicaragua decision is of relatively little, if any, utility in this particular case. It's the submission of the Prosecutor that the proper test for determining whether or not a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions has been committed involves assessing the relevant provisions of international humanitarian law, particularly, the Geneva Conventions themselves, and applying these provisions to the facts as they existed at the appropriate time in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It is this single argument which the Prosecution will focus on in this oral argument. In the indictment, Dusko Tadic is alleged to have committed grave breaches in Bosnia against Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat civilians between about the 23rd of May, 1992 and about the 31st of December, 1992. It is submitted that the relevant questions which must be answered are, and there are six of them: First, were Bosnia and the other relevant State, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, legally bound by the Geneva Conventions as a matter of treaty or customary law between about the 23rd of May, 1992 and the 31st of December, 1992? Second, did a situation exist in Bosnia during the relevant period such that the applicability of the Civilians Convention was triggered as a result of either Common Article 2 or Article 6 of the Civilians Convention? Third, was Tadic linked to one side or one high contracting party? Fourth, were the victims linked to another side or high contracting party? Fifth, did the victims constitute protected persons under one of the Geneva Conventions with respect to Tadic and the side to which he was linked? Sixth, did Tadic commit an act prescribed as a grave breach under the applicable Geneva Convention? It is the submission of the Prosecution that the answer to each of these six questions is "Yes," and I will run through why we consider that to be the position now.
