First, Bosnia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were legally bound by the Geneva Conventions as a matter of both customary and treaty law during the period covered by the indictment. Second, an international armed conflict continued to exist between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia throughout 1992, and as a result of this, the grave breach provisions were potentially applicable throughout the territory of Bosnia and the FRY during this period. If I might quote, in part, paragraph 70 of the majority decision in the Tadic jurisdiction appeal, and I'll just quote the parts referring to international armed conflict: "We find that an armed conflict exists whenever there is a resort to armed force between States. International humanitarian law applies from the initiation of such armed conflicts and extends beyond the cessation of hostilities until a general conclusion of peace is reached. Until that moment, international humanitarian law continues to apply in the whole territory of the warring States, whether or not actual combat takes place there." The Red Cross commentary on Geneva Convention 4 adopts a similar, very broad view: "Any difference arising between two States and leading to the intervention of members of the armed forces is an armed conflict within the meaning of Article 2." It is submitted that the SFRY/FRY is a party to an international armed conflict with Bosnia on the basis that, first, the Trial Chamber itself found that until the 19th of May, 1992, the Yugoslav national army was involved in an international armed conflict with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thereafter the VJ, the renamed Yugoslav army, was directly involved in an armed conflict against Bosnia. If we accept that the Yugoslav armed forces continued to be involved in the conflict after the 19th of May, 1992, we have an international armed conflict. There is no other legal conclusion that can possibly be drawn. Further, there is no indication of a general conclusion of peace before the Dayton Agreement in 1995. If I might refer briefly to some paragraphs of the trial decision in the Tadic case, part of paragraph 118 of the majority decision: "VJ aircrew and aircraft remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the May withdrawal and worked with the VRS throughout 1992 and 1993." Paragraph 119: "The Podgorica Corps of what had been the JNA and was now the VJ remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina for much of 1992 and, under the command of General Perisic, was involved in the killing of Muslims and Croats in the Mostar region." Paragraph 569, in part: "The forces of the VJ continued to be involved in the armed conflict after that date." That date was the 19th of May. One does not have an international armed conflict occurring in part of a country. If we have combat forces deployed in combat in Bosnia by the Yugoslav government after the 19th of May, 1992, we have an international armed conflict. The third question which had been posed was: Was Tadic linked to one side or one high contracting party in the conflict? It is submitted that Tadic was linked to the FRY side in the international armed conflict between the FRY and Bosnia. Dusko Tadic was born in Bosnia and is of Serb ethnicity. He was actively involved in Serb nationalist politics. He was employed as a reserve policeman. The activities which are the subject of the indictment occurred in areas controlled by Bosnian Serb forces, the VRS. Tadic was linked to the RS, the Republika Srpska, and the VRS, in the sense that the RS was his entity and the VRS was the army of his entity. In turn, the RS and the VRS were linked to and on the same side as the VJ and the FRY. The evidence shows that throughout 1992, Republika Srpska was a self-proclaimed entity within Bosnia that regarded itself as part of the FRY. In particular, the evidence shows that in May 1992, the SDS, that being the ruling political party in Republika Srpska, did not seek to be separated from the FRY. Its relationship with the FRY at that time cannot be characterised as one of "merely coordinating political activities" as they were by the Trial Chamber. Further, the VRS should be regarded as being on the same side as the VJ in an international conflict with the Bosnian army. It was accepted by the Trial Chamber that the redesignation of a part of the JNA as the VRS was deliberately planned by the authorities in Belgrade to create the semblance of the withdrawal of FRY forces from the territory of Bosnia. This creation did not come as an immediate response to Security Council Resolution 752 of 1992. The evidence does not point to an independent initiative on the part of the Bosnian Serbs to form a breakaway irregular military force. The creation of the VRS by the FRY therefore does not indicate any indication or any intention by Belgrade to relinquish control of part of its own army; rather, establishment of the VRS was undertaken in pursuit of Yugoslavia's own objectives. The evidence demonstrates that these objectives were implemented by political and military operations that were controlled by Belgrade and the Yugoslav National Army. There is no evidence to suggest that these objectives changed on the 19th of May, 1992. In fact, the Trial Chamber found that they remained unaltered. Given that the FRY's pursuit of its political and military objectives continued beyond the 19th of May in much the same manner as before, no reasonable basis exists for inferring a factual loss of control over the VRS. It would have been illogical for Belgrade to relinquish its control of its entire military operation in Bosnia in 1992 when, after extensive preparations, the operations had only begun to be implemented. The high level of planning and preparation in 1991 and early 1992, as noted by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 80 to 146 of its judgement, did, however, permit less explicit forms of command over military operations to be practised, and these were adopted especially as a response to increased international scrutiny. As the evidence establishes, the renaming of the JNA forces in Bosnia was one of the FRY's main strategies for responding to international demands while, at the same time, taking advantage of the extensive preparations that had already been undertaken. From a purely practical point of view, JNA military operations, under the command of Belgrade that had already commenced by the 19th of May, 1992, would not have been able to cease overnight in any event. It is normal, when military operations are planned, that military commanders are thinking at the very least a few days ahead of time. The people on the front line, the people involved in immediate operations, are probably thinking with a very short time frame. Those back at the core level or more senior level normally are expected to be planning for things two or three days away. The take-over of Kozarac certainly was not something that wasn't planned well before the 19th of May, 1992. The Trial Chamber had before it sufficient evidence of a chain of military command between Belgrade and Pale. The Trial Chamber accepted that General Mladic, formerly of the JNA, was appointed by Belgrade as the commander of the VRS. The evidence shows that he and the VRS main staff continued to implement the JNA's military objectives and operations in Bosnia and were provided with broad operational control to achieve this end under the overall command of Belgrade. The Trial Chamber did accept that the VRS main staff had links and regular communications with Belgrade. I might draw your particular attention to the Trial Chamber judgement at page 221, paragraph 598 in that respect. The evidence may not disclose the exact details of how the VRS related to the main command in Belgrade or that General Mladic and the VRS command openly received regular orders from Belgrade. As the testimony of one of the witnesses for the Prosecution, James Gow, demonstrated, however, a clear intention existed to mask the commanding role of the FRY. This explains the evidence of Colonel Selak which was relied upon by the Trial Chamber in finding that the relationship between Belgrade and Pale was characterised by a level of coordination only. That is what the Trial Chamber decided at paragraph 598. It is submitted that the intention of Belgrade was to make it seem as if their links with Pale were as partners acting only in cooperation with one another. The groundwork had been completed by the JNA for launching extensive military operations in Bosnia, and certain aspects had already been implemented. As the Trial Chamber pointed out, these operations unfolded with significant success during the summer and autumn of 1992, and this in itself testifies to a degree to the control that was maintained over military affairs in Bosnia by the FRY. From a number of additional factors, further inferences can be drawn of effective military control over the VRS by Belgrade. The FRY/VJ created the VRS, and the structures and ranks of the VRS and the VJ were identical. The FRY/VJ directed and supervised the activities and operations of the VRS. As a result, the VRS reflected the strategies and tactics devised by the FRY and the VJ. The FRY and its army, the VJ, directly intervened in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the 19th of May, 1992, and was fighting alongside the VRS and providing critical combat support to it. The FRY/VJ provided extensive financial, logistical, and other assistance and support to the VRS. If I may, I would like to quote from a paragraph, or part of a paragraph, of the Trial Chamber majority judgement. This is part of paragraph 115, and it talks about things that were happening around about the 19th of May, 1992: "Although then formerly members of the VRS --" This is after the 19th of May. "-- rather than of the former JNA, they continued to receive their salaries from the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro, and the pensions of those who in due course retired were paid by that government. At a briefing of officers concerned with logistics, General Djordje Jukic, then of the VRS but who had, until the 18th of May, 1992, been chief of staff of the technical administration of the JNA in Belgrade, announced that all the active duty members of the VRS would continue to be paid by the federal government in Belgrade which would continue to finance the VRS as it had the JNA with the same numerical strengths of officers as were registered in the 19th of May, 1992." It is conventional wisdom among international lawyers that mere logistical support or financial support provided to a group does not necessarily indicate participation in the conflict. That may be so if what we were talking about is something like, say, the provision of lend/lease support by the United States to the United Kingdom during World War II. No one would suggest either before or after Pearl Harbour that the Americans controlled or were intimately involved on the British side as such just because of financial support. This is not what we are talking about here. We are talking about a country paying its soldiers to perform a task in another country. Not only continuing to pay them but providing them with a pension after its all over. This is not mere logistical support. This is proof, it is submitted, that the VRS, or at least this corps of officers, its cadre of officers, its most experienced professionals, were, in fact, performing tasks for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The paymaster controls in this particular case. Most armed forces, when and if they, for example, second soldiers or officers to other armed forces for a period of time, they do so under conditions whereby, if those forces to which they are seconded are engaged in hostilities, that automatically terminates the period of secondment. You go back home. Because if you stay there as a member of your country's armed forces in somebody else's war, somebody else is quite likely to come to the conclusion that your country is also engaged in the armed conflict. Well, here, despite the mask, despite what perhaps may be a different label, despite what may perhaps be different uniforms, you have the same paymaster continuing throughout somebody's professional career. People retire to Belgrade, they get their pensions from Yugoslavia. This is nothing but the VJ, the Yugoslav army, under another name. In summary, it is the submission of the Prosecution that Tadic was linked to the RS and the VRS, and they, in turn, were linked so inextricably to the FRY and the VJ that all can be regarded as on the FRY side. In the words of paragraph 209 of the Celebici decision: "Should the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina be international, the relevant norms of international humanitarian law apply throughout its territory until the general cessation of hostilities unless it can be shown that the conflicts in some areas were separate internal conflicts unrelated to the larger international conflict." Here there was an international conflict at the appropriate time between the FRY and Bosnia. The fighting between the VRS and the Bosnian army was a part of that conflict. The fourth question which I had suggested should be posed is: Were the victims linked to another side, another high contracting party? In this particular case, yes, most emphatically. The victim group constituted Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. Their government was engaged in an international armed conflict with the FRY. Did the victims -- and this is the fifth question -- did the victims constitute "protected persons" under one of the Geneva Conventions with respect to Tadic and the side to which he was linked? The answer, once again, is "Yes." The victims were civilians. They were protected under the civilians convention. They were in the hands of the FRY and they did not have the nationality of the FRY. Last, did Tadic commit grave breaches under the civilians convention? Yes. The criminal liability of the appellant, we submit, has been more than adequately established on the basis of the record. For that reason, it is the submission of the Prosecution that Tadic can and should be held criminally liable for the Article 2 counts. That concludes my oral argument with reference to ground number 1. I will turn, unless there are questions, to ground number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, just one question. Is my impression correct that your briefs on this ground suggested a criterion which may be described as a criterion of a demonstrable link being applicable? Have you dealt with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It was my view, Your Honour, that what I had done in this outlining of the different questions was intended to demonstrate how one constituted that demonstrable link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You meant to build --

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- on that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then my only remaining question is whether there is any specific authority for that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: We are dealing -- I wouldn't want to say we're entirely making new law here, Your Honour, but what we are doing is trying to apply the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, and I think we have got to try, to the extent its practicable, find all the answers within the Geneva Conventions themselves or by means of extrapolation from the Geneva Conventions. If I might try the reverse side of this? There is certainly more-than-adequate case law to demonstrate that the accused needs no more than a demonstrable link with his side in a conflict. For example, there are post World War II war crimes cases where we are talking about the perpetrators being members of a lynch mob. We have got post World War II cases where the accused would be, say, someone perhaps of the same nationality as the victim but nevertheless employed or acting in a position of some administrative authority in a concentration camp. We have got a lot of evidence for the other side, for the perpetrator side, I think being regarded as where the demonstrable link comes in. I am unaware of any case law which specifically adverts to the kinds of issues we've got here. What I have been doing after a fashion is turning the existing case law upside down, and I think the argument applies going in the opposite direction. I wish I could be more helpful, but frankly this is not an area which has been covered a lot in the case law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then I understand you to be saying that the burden of your submissions is that the facts establish a demonstrable link and your submission in law is that a demonstrable link is an acceptable juridical criterion?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, essentially. If I may just elaborate a little bit? One can look at things -- for example, the Encyclopaedia of Public International Law. When it discusses what constitutes a war crime, it talks about a war crime being something which is committed by someone who is an agent of one side against either a neutral person or a national of the opposing side in a conflict. In fact, it is my submission that, unfortunately, the author of that provision got it demonstrably wrong because it is very easy to demonstrate that there is no need for an agency relationship between the perpetrator of a war crime and the state, the entity, on behalf of which he acts. For starters, if one always had to be an agent, a relatively convenient defence would be saying, "Well, my armed forces ordered me not to do this, my government ordered me not to do this. I just did it anyway." But to get beyond that which may look, to a degree, facetious, there certainly are cases such as the Essen lynching case, for example, where the perpetrators of the offence constituted a lynch mob, and I don't think a lynch mob would normally be regarded as acting as an agent on behalf of the government where it is located. So it is that kind of reasoning, one would wish there was more case law to support it, but these are unprecedented circumstances we are trying to address here to a degree, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: To sum it up, your submission is that, as between the VRS and Yugoslavia, there were three relevant criteria: One, effective control; failing that, agency; failing that, a demonstrable link. Is that a way of encapsulating your arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Very much so, Your Honour. Of course, the briefs also address the effective control and the agency arguments. It was the demonstrable link which I thought was more appropriate to endeavour to discuss here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What you're saying is that the last one, a demonstrable link, would encompass the other two criteria?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I would word it slightly differently in that I would suggest that a demonstrable link is, first of all, the appropriate test in the circumstances, and the other two would not be so appropriate. But I would also submit and, in fact, concede that the effective control standard and the agency standard are both somewhat higher standards than the demonstrable link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you're correct, shouldn't I understand you to mean that the last criterion, a demonstrable link, is wide enough to include the other two criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes. Very much so. That's what I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then you may proceed to your next ground. My colleague would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you could be of some assistance to us because I think I agree with you that no link is required when you have a war crime by a civilian. You quoted the Essen lynching case. Now, civilians may commit war crimes, but for a civilian to commit a grave breach, you have to prove that there's a link between that particular civilian and a belligerent. Otherwise, a civilian may commit a war crime within an internal armed conflict and it is a war crime or within the framework of an international armed conflict, but for a civilian or anybody who has no official capacity, who is not a member of the armed forces, to commit a grave breach, you have to show the link between the armed forces and a belligerent or a foreign power taking part in the international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I would be inclined to disagree with that. I agree that we're clearly talking about a different situation if what we're talking about is an internal armed conflict or an international armed conflict, but it would be the submission of the Prosecution that the kinds of standards which came out of the post-World War II cases would be applicable in an international armed conflict - and it is in an international armed conflict - but in an international armed conflict to both other kinds of war crimes and grave breaches. If what we were doing was discussing internal armed conflict, perhaps it might be a little different, but I think the standard linkage for war crimes in an international armed conflicts and for grave breaches would be basically the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Still, I fail to see how, within the framework of an international armed conflict, somebody who is not a member of the armed forces or one of the belligerents may be accused of a grave breach and not of a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I would have no difficulty doing that at all, Your Honour. As an example, and we'll purify the situation somewhat by saying, let us suppose we have a prisoner of war in Yugoslavia from Bosnia. I would submit that if a Yugoslav civilian killed that prisoner of war, he would have committed a grave breach. He need not be affiliated with the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question: I am afraid I don't have the text of the Geneva Conventions close at hand, but I remember in the IV Geneva Conventions, there is a provision, a common provision, whereby in case of a grave breach, of course, individual criminal responsibility may arise for the perpetrator of a grave breach, but at the same time, also the State to which that particular person belongs may bear international responsibility. So you have two notions: state responsibility and individual criminal responsibility for the same action. Therefore, if this is correct, I fail to see how you may say that the Nicaragua case only applies to State responsibility and not to individual criminal responsibility. I think the Nicaragua case test applies to the criteria for attributing a particular act committed by an individual to a State if the individual is acting on behalf of the State. Again, we fall back on the notion of agent or State official, a de facto organ, to use the terminology of the International Law Commission on State responsibility, acts committed by private persons acting not in their official capacity but as individuals who act on behalf of a state. Therefore, you have one test applicable to both State responsibility and individual criminal responsibility. This is my proposition, but I would like to have your comments. I may be totally wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: With respect, if I may at least disagree to some extent. First of all, yes, there is a provision -- I was trying to thumb through and I couldn't find it either -- concerning the State responsibility, but I would suggest there are some circumstances where you would have State responsibility for persons who have committed grave breaches and others where you most emphatically would not. I don't know. If, for example, you had an armed force which had an elaborate law of armed conflict, training programme, an elaborate monitoring system, took all appropriate means to ensure disciplinary action, ensured that its troops were ordered not to commit offences, and then you had a soldier, for example, commit an offence or commit a grave breach, I don't think the State would necessarily be held responsible for that. I think you would have individual criminal responsibility. I don't know if you would automatically have State responsibility. With reference to the Nicaragua decision, the Nicaragua decision is certainly concerned with State responsibility. I don't know if I would suggest that the kind of criteria that it talks about, it's submitted by the Prosecution, would have some relevance to determining whether or not you've got an international armed conflict or the applicability of the grave breach provisions. But it would be our submission that that is perhaps more applicable when you're talking about a situation where really what you've got is a rebel or insurgent group functioning in the territory of another state and what you're trying to do is to determine the responsibility of another State. I mean, the real Nicaragua situation, to what extent is the U.S. responsible for the activities of the Contras? If what you've got and what we submit here we do have is an international armed conflict involving combat units from Yugoslavia, it would be the submission of the Prosecution that we need not rely on the Nicaragua test or the Nicaragua tests, to be more accurate, as an exclusive means for determining whether or not the actions of individual accused can be referred to as grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, if I understand you correctly, your proposition is that whenever you have, say, in a case the possibility of two parallel conflicts, an internal armed conflict plus an international armed conflict, the rules relating to the international armed conflict in a way embrace and cover any event, even those committed within the framework of the civil war? So everything would be covered by the grave breach provisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That was not -- at least it was not intended to be our submission, Your Honour. To use the wording of the Celebici decision, if you've got clearly separate internal armed conflicts, then certainly you wouldn't be talking about grave breaches and you wouldn't be applying the law for international armed conflict. For example, in Bosnia, the conflict between the Bosnian government and the Fikret Abdic faction, I don't think there's any way in which we could talk about grave breaches in connection with that. But when what we're talking about is really, we would submit, a clear international armed conflict between Yugoslavia and Bosnia with the VRS or the Republika Srpska on the same side and with many links to the Yugoslav government, we would submit that it would be entirely appropriate to apply the grave breaches there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might ask your help on this point: At all material times, say you, Yugoslavia had fighting forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both before the 19th of May and after the 19th of May. Why then did the majority find that after the 19th of May there was no armed conflict between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia? Have I got the facts wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I believe you have the facts correctly, Your Honour. My understanding would be that the majority misapplied the view of the Appeals Chamber as expressed in the Tadic jurisdiction decision. Although they used the words, for some reason or another instead of saying, "Once you've got combat forces involved in the country, you've got an international armed conflict and it affects the whole country," they said, "Well, okay, the Yugoslav army has withdrawn," or to be more accurate, "The Yugoslav army has divided," but they themselves, they're the ones -- I mean, when I was quoting those paragraphs from the decision, that wasn't me. That was them, their findings, that Yugoslav combat forces continued to be engaged in Bosnia. I think what they did was instead of looking on the law as something which applies to the whole territory, they looked on it as, "Well, you can have an international armed conflict going on in this little corner of Bosnia, but up here at this end, here you still don't have the umbrella international armed conflict applying." To me, the law applies to -- once you have an international armed conflict, it applies to the whole territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. They then, according to you, adopted a compartmentalised approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Very much so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Will you pass to your next ground then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, sir. The third ground, which I would intend to address somewhat more briefly, is the finding that crimes against humanity cannot be committed for purely personal motives. This finding does not affect the verdict against the accused. We concede it does not strictly fall within the wording of section 25(1)(a) of the Statute, in that we're not talking about an error on a question of law which invalidates the decision as such. That being said, it is our submission that what we're talking about is a significant question of law that is of general importance to the Tribunal's jurisprudence which it is possible for the Court to correct on appeal and which should be corrected on appeal. It's our submission that if this finding stands, it is, unfortunately, persuasive authority for other Trial Chambers, both of this Tribunal and for the ICTR. If it's followed in other cases, it could result in unjustified and legally erroneous acquittals. That is the reason why we would wish to see this issue considered on appeal, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That concludes your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Well, that concludes why we wish, but we do have a bit more on why we think it's wrong. Do you wish me to proceed further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Indeed. Article 5 of the Statute mandates that crimes against humanity within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal must be committed in armed conflict. The Trial Chamber found that these words require that there be a nexus between the perpetrator's acts or omissions and the armed conflict. As to the nature of the nexus required, the Trial Chamber found that, subject to two caveats, it is sufficient for purposes of crimes against humanity that the act occurred in the course or duration of an armed conflict. The first caveat was that the act be linked geographically as well as temporally with the armed conflict, which is, of course, quite appropriate. The second caveat was that the act and the armed conflict be related or at least that the act not be unrelated to the armed conflict. The Trial Chamber then went on to hold that the requirement that the act not be unrelated involved two aspects: First, the perpetrator must know of the broader context in which the act occurs. Second, the act must not be taken for purely personal motives unrelated to the armed conflict. The Prosecution, as indicated, challenges the Trial Chamber's finding that, to fall within Article 5, the act must not be taken for purely personal motives. Nothing in Article 5 itself suggests it contains a requirement that crimes against humanity cannot be committed for purely personal reasons, nor is there such a suggestion in the Secretary-General's report on the Statute or in the Security Council debates related to the adoption of the Statute. It is submitted that the weight of authority supports the proposition that crimes against humanity can be committed for purely personal reasons. The only authority which the Trial Chamber directly relies upon is a 1948 case from the post Second World War trials before German courts, and that case, it is submitted, in fact, contradicts the Trial Chamber's conclusion. In that case, the defendants had denounced a Jewish victim to the Gestapo for her anti-Nazi remarks. The Jewish victim subsequently died in a concentration camp. The defendant's sole motive for denunciation was to "get rid of the victim" because they were unhappy with her hysterical behaviour. Applying the provisions of Control Council Law 10, the Court found that, despite the purely personal motives underlying the conduct of the defendants, their behaviour could still be characterised as a crime against humanity. To quote, in part, an unofficial translation, the defendant's conduct "was intimately linked to the national socialist regime of violence and arbitrariness because, from the very outset, it clearly fit into the organised campaign of persecution against all Jews and everything Jewish in Canada." Not in Canada. I'm sorry. That's a nationalist bias there or lack of it. "... everything Jewish in Germany." Now, what happened here was something which was done for purely personal reasons. The people involved had no desire except to "get rid of" the wife of one of them, and they denounced that person to the Gestapo as a result of that. We say that the court, in that particular case, did not suggest that there was any requirement that the defendant's motives not be purely personal. In fact, they accepted that they were purely personal. It is submitted that it is inconsistent with the humanitarian object and purpose of our Statute to leave unpunished acts forming part of a widespread or systematic attack against civilian populations simply because they were committed for purely personal motives. Such a requirement would create an expedient justification for perpetrators of large scale crimes allowing them to escape liability. It is submitted that when you are considering the requirement of non-personal motives for crimes against humanity, it is important to define the term "motive" as something distinct from "intent" or "knowledge." The term "motive," it is understood, is sometimes used in some civil law systems to refer to a form of special intent. For example, the concept of absicht, and I wish I could pronounce that properly, at least it's spelled "A-B-S-I-C-H-T," under German law refers to an intensified or a direct intention which may be equated with motivation whereby the offender wants a specific result. But we're not talking about a form of special intent here. What we're talking about is the kind of situation where what's at issue is the ultimate reason perhaps for the accused to perform an act. For example, it doesn't matter whether or not an accused steals money in order to buy Christmas presents for his poor children or to support a heroin habit. All we're concerned with is that he stole and he intended to steal, and what we're concerned with, it is submitted here, is the same sort of thing. There's no requirement for non-personal motive beyond knowledge of the context of a widespread or systematic act into which an accused's act fits. The Prosecutor is submitting that, as a general proposition and one which is applicable here, motives are simply irrelevant in criminal law. It does not matter if an accused committed inhumane acts for reasons that are purely personal, for example, getting rid of a Muslim neighbour to whom he owes money, so long as he or she has the requisite knowledge of the context. If this Chamber upholds the decision of the Trial Chamber, it is submitted it will establish a new and unnecessary additional element for crimes against humanity. It will become necessary to establish motive as well as intent and the other existing elements. That's the argument on the third ground by the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, let me ask you one question. Do we have a problem here of the meaning which the majority wished to ascribe to the words "purely personal"? Did the majority accept or reject the German case to which you referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: My recollection, Your Honour, is that they viewed it as supporting their position concerning "purely personal," and we would submit that, in fact, it is contrary to their holding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there a possibility of interpreting the majority judgement to mean that they were talking of purely personal reasons otherwise than as indicated in the German case? There you had the word "fit." The man removed his wife from the scene, denounced her, I think. He had knowledge of the general final solution policy. Although he acted for purely personal reasons, he not only had knowledge of that general policy but he meant to connect the purely personal with the policy. He meant to use the policy to implement his personal objectives; am I not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I would think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well now, I understand the Trial Chamber, the majority, to be accepting that situation. Then they moved further. Let me say I am asking questions; I am not digging in my heels and I am not stating a position. This is a possible interpretation. Having accepted that decision, they then moved a little further and said: If you are acting for purely personal reasons with knowledge of the system but not intending that what you are doing fits into the system, not intending that what you are doing should utilise the system, then that is a case not caught by the definition of crimes against humanity. Do you think that is a possible interpretation? Take the case instanced by Mr. Clegg of the man killing another man for the reason that, while this other man was a schoolmaster, he had beaten him up. Let us assume that the assailant in that case knew of the policy but did not intend to utilise the policy. Would that, you think, be the kind of situation which the majority had in mind when it spoke of "purely personal reasons"? You know of the policy and you commit a crime, but you do not intend that the commission of the crime should fit into the policy or should make any use of the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that if an individual dislikes his teacher, who happens to be a Muslim and, for that reason, he informs the Serb authorities, who come and pick up the school teacher and take him away and mistreat him in some way or other or kill him, it is submitted that that would be a circumstance where we would be thinking we don't have -- that would come within the kind of guidelines that are talked about in that decision. If what we are talking about, however, is a person who goes and beats his teacher because of personal resentment, I don't think the situation is or should be legally any different. The only difference is that in the situation where he does it himself, he does it himself. In both cases, it is being done in a permissive environment which he knows exists. He knows that what is happening here is the government or the political authorities are not going to punish him in any way and he is taking advantage of the existence of that system. For that reason, it would be the submission of the Prosecution that, no, in the kind of case that Mr. Clegg referred to, assuming that we have knowledge of the widespread or systematic attacks being directed against the civilian population, we still should have criminal culpability for an Article 5 offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are talking of situations in which the accused has knowledge on the general policy and is acting for personal reasons but also intends that his personal actions should call upon the general system either for protection or for implementation. Now, was that the situation which the majority had in mind or did they have in mind a model under which the accused commits a crime, such as murder, with knowledge of the general system but not intending in any way to connect the general system with the crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It would be our submission that as long as he is "taking a benefit" from the existence of the system, it should not be something which is not punishable under Article 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that, but I am putting to you another model, a model under which he knows of the policy, he commits a crime, but there is no linkage between one and the other. He doesn't intend to "take a benefit," to use your words. He commits a simple crime. All that happens is that he has knowledge of this general policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It would be our submission that knowledge is all he needs, Your Honour, and nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Even if he intends in no way to connect the one with the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: De facto he is receiving a benefit after a fashion. I mean, he may successfully conceal the body so that the political authorities never become aware of what has happened or anything like that, but it would be our submission that as long as he knows of the existence of the system and he takes an act, it is virtually impossible or extremely difficult to separate the knowledge from the crime, and the knowledge, we would submit, is what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I am asking you is, what was the model which you think the majority had in mind? Did the majority have in mind a model under which the accused knew of the general policy, committed the crime and intended it, that the commission of that crime should in some way benefit from the policy, or did the majority have in mind a situation in which the accused knew the general policy, committed the crime, but intended in no way to connect the two, having acted for purely personal reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I would imagine that the majority had in mind the second option, but we would submit that, in fact, with the knowledge basically comes all that is needed for the link to the armed conflict. Because of the knowledge, you have got what you need for that linkage. Now, there are, of course, many things which must be established before we have criminal culpability, but insofar as the link to the armed conflict is needed, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Should I understand you to mean that theoretically you understand the kind of model which I believe the majority might have had in mind, but what you are saying is the factual situation would tend to override that model?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps for policy reasons, because it may provide a plausible excuse but an unjustified one, it is one which the Court should pay little heed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, my colleague on my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Just to support what Mr. Fenrick has just said. Actually, I am aware of about 20 to 25 German cases about denunciations, and some of those cases support your proposition. What is required is the action by the perpetrators, denunciation of a Jew or a political opponent to Gestapo or the other police corps, and the knowledge that there is persecution against political opponents or Jews. No intention is required. The objective link between the act of denunciation and the general oppressive policy of the national socialist regime was sufficient. So therefore I feel that this interpretation is the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I am very grateful to my colleague for that explanation. It is, however, a model which I would classify as belonging to instances in which the accused not only knows of the policy but intends to call upon the policy to cover his crime because he is making a denunciation and the denunciation has to be given effect to by the instrumentalities which control the policy. The model I was putting to you was one which I believed it was possible that the majority had in mind, a model in which the accused knew the policy, committed his crime, the crime might not have been one involving denunciation at all, and so he intended in no way that his crime should benefit in any way from the policy. Do you follow the model which I am putting to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand the model which my colleague has in mind, but I have a different model in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I find it very difficult to envisage a practical application of that sort of thing. I would think perhaps it would be somewhat unlikely as a practical case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. Well then, it is two minutes past the hour. Shall we adjourn at this point and resume in half an hour's time? At 4.30? I know we should resume at 4.20. Four twenty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ready with your next ground, Mr. Fenrick?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes indeed, Your Honour. The next ground is ground number 4. The Prosecution is appealing against a finding by the Trial Chamber that all crimes against humanity require a discriminatory intent. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that all crimes against humanity enumerated under Article 5 require a discriminatory intent. Because of this finding, the Trial Chamber restricted the scope of persecutions under sub-paragraph (H) only to those acts not charged elsewhere in the indictment under Article 5 rather than imposing additional liability for all acts committed on discriminatory grounds. In doing so, it would appear that the sentence against the accused was significantly reduced. It is submitted that there is no express requirement for a discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity in the chapeau of Article 5 of the Tribunal Statute. The inclusion of such a requirement under the corresponding Article 3 of the Statute of the Rwanda Tribunal applies a contrario that there was no intention to impose a similar requirement under the Statute of this Tribunal. Further, there is no requirement of discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity under international customary law. Indeed, the Trial Chamber conceded that neither the Nuremberg Charter nor Control Council Law No. 10 nor the Tokyo Tribunal Statute, all of which provide a basis, after a fashion, for Article 5, contain any provision imposing a discriminatory requirement for all crimes against humanity. Indeed, all of these provisions distinguish between two types of crimes against humanity, murder-type crimes, such as murder, extermination, or enslavement, and persecution-type crimes committed on political, racial, or religious grounds. Further, this distinction has been reaffirmed under Article 7 of the International Criminal Court Statute which expressly rejects a requirement of discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity. It is submitted that as a general rule, provisions of the Statute defining crimes should be interpreted as reflecting customary international law unless an intention to deviate from customary international law is express from the terms of the Statute. Here, because of an unambiguous customary law norm that there is no requirement for discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity, the commentary of the Secretary-General and the interpretative statements of three Security Council Members should not be attributed authoritative weight in construing the scope of Article 5. It is our submission that a presumption exists whereby the Statute should be read in conformity with international conventional or customary law in the absence of an express intent manifested in the Statute to deviate therefrom. The Security Council may modify existing norms but, if so, it is submitted that they must be explicit. For example, Article 5 of the Statute requires a nexus with armed conflict for crimes against humanity. This does not violate the nullum crimen principle and certainly is explicit and it is a narrowing of the customary law norm. Your Honours might recollect that reference was made to statements of Security Council members in the Tadic jurisdiction decision. In interpreting Article 3 of the Statute so that it included Common Article 3 within its scope, reference was made to the text of the provision in Article 3 which provided that laws or customs of war should include but not be limited to certain enumerated offences. The interpretative statements of the Security Council members were then invoked in order to determine the scope of crimes that were covered by this illustrative provision. It is submitted, however, that at that time those interpretative statements were secondary sources in the interpretation of express provisions in the Statute. It is our submission that relying on interpretative statements to include discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity, when Article 5 does not contain any such requirement, would be the equivalent of relying on such statements to argue, for example, that Article 3 is exhaustive when, in fact, it is illustrative. It is our submission that factual precedents, unfortunately, are often confused with law. The common conception of crimes against humanity involves the persecution of Jews in Nazi Germany, Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Albanians in Kosovo today. Since most historical precedents do, in fact, involve discriminatory grounds, there may be an erroneous assumption that such grounds are required as a matter of law. It is our submission that the rules of statutory interpretation also militate against requiring a discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity. Such a requirement would relegate the crime of persecution under Article 5(H) to a mere residual provision. Furthermore, it would also make other inhumane acts under Article 5(I) redundant. It is suggested that the Statute should be interpreted in order to give proper effect to all of its provisions. The requirement of discriminatory intent for all crimes against humanity is inconsistent with the humanitarian object and purpose of the Statute and international humanitarian law. It would create, for example, a significant normative lacuna by failing to protect civilian populations not listed in the grounds of discrimination. The Rome Statute, as was indicated, does not make any reference to discriminatory intent as a requirement underlying all of the different forms of crimes against humanity. This instrument is the product of a prolonged and laborious process of deliberation among Member States of the U.N. and other interested parties. Reference to specific discriminatory grounds can only be found in relation to the specific crimes of persecution, Article 7(1)(H), Article 7(2)(F), which has to do with affecting the ethnic composition of a population, forced pregnancy under Article 7(2)(F), apartheid under Article 7(2)(H) and enforced disappearance of persons under 7(2)(I). It can only be concluded that the International Community thus considered that, as a general rule, crimes against humanity do not require any particular discriminatory intent or motive except in the case of certain specific types of crime against humanity. It is our submission that the overwhelming weight of authority, in fact, supports the proposition that there is no requirement for a discriminatory intent or discriminatory grounds for all crimes against humanity. That closes the submission of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, should I understand you to mean this, that absent the Secretary-General's report, absent the three interpretative declarations, the Statute falls to be read in accordance with existing customary international law, and that when so read, it does not include a general requirement for proof of discriminatory intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, could you help the Bench on one point? There is some literature on interpretative declarations in relation to multi-lateral treaties. Can you help us with any literature on the subject of interpretative declarations in relation to Security Council resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot, Your Honour. We are familiar enough about interpretation of statutes and interpretation of treaties, but I am not aware of anything which specifically refers to interpretation of Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I haven't found any either, but I thought I might profit from the occasion by picking your brain, and counsel on the other side would, at the appropriate time, make a contribution on the subject, I imagine. Now you will pass to your next ground then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That is the end of my grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Before you take your seat, would you care to respond to a point which I had put to you at the beginning concerning ground 3, I think? I believe in your brief you recognised that it does not impact on any of the concrete reliefs for which you pray, and I caution by repeating that at this point I have no particular position, but I wanted to know whether you had any, whether you had any learning to put to us on that subject, on the receivability of this point having regard to your concession that it does not have any practical impact on the actual reliefs which you seek but you are seeking a pronouncement because of the general importance of the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, I have nothing to add to what I said at the time in connection with ground 3, and all we had to say at that time was that we considered it to be a significant question of law of general importance which should be addressed on appeal and that if it stood, it might very well have an adverse persuasive effect on other decisions of the Tribunal. But those are our points in connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you. Judge Mumba? The bench understands you. Then it would be Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, as my colleague indicated, I would be addressing Prosecution grounds of appeal 2 and 5. Ground 2 is the Prosecution appeal which asks you to reverse the Trial Chamber's finding of not guilty on counts 30 and 31 involving the killings of five men in the village of Jaskici. We've had a somewhat related issue this morning in the appellant's presentation when we discussed with you their ground number 3, but we suggest to you that there is a significant difference in the two grounds for appeal. In appellant's ground number 3, the appellant was basically asking you to go behind the Trial Chamber's finding of fact and, indeed, to find that the findings of fact were erroneous. In our request and our submission, in ground 2, we are not asking you to do that. We accept the findings of fact of the Trial Chamber; we accept them fully. We do not ask you to go behind their findings and make a different assessment of the credibility of the evidence. Our position for ground 2 is that, while finding the appropriate facts, the Trial Chamber erred in two different ways. First of all, the Trial Chamber erred by the way it applied the law of proof beyond reasonable doubt to the facts that it found and, secondly, that in reaching its determination that we had failed to meet our burden of proof beyond reasonable doubt, the Trial Chamber also erred in its application of the principle of common purpose or common criminal enterprise. I will address those in the order I have just mentioned them. First of all, Your Honour, we suggest that when it reached its decision in this case, the Trial Chamber erred in the way that it applied the test of proof beyond reasonable doubt. We suggest further that in deciding whether the Prosecution has proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt and in testing whether the Trial Chamber erred in concluding we had not met that burden, that the Appellate Chamber must look at the facts and all reasonable inferences that can be drawn from the facts that were found. Guilt is proven beyond a reasonable doubt if, looking at the facts that are accepted as reliable evidence, the only reasonable explanation or conclusion from those facts is that of guilt. On the other hand, reasonable doubt is not created by bare possibility or by suggestion or by surmise. Reasonable doubt exists only when, looking at the evidence, there is a rational and fair doubt as to guilt of the accused. Looking at the language that the Trial Chamber used in reaching its determination that we had failed in our burden, the Prosecution suggests that that language demonstrates the Trial Chamber's erroneous application of the test for proof beyond reasonable doubt. That language is found in paragraph 373 at page 133 of the findings of fact, and at that point, the Trial Chamber indicated that: "The bare possibility that the deaths of the Jaskici villagers were the result of encountering a part of that large force," and here they are speaking of the large force that entered Sivci, "would be enough in the state of evidence, or, rather, the lack of it, relating to their deaths, to prevent satisfaction beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was involved in those deaths." That's the first ground that they use for finding that we failed to prove our case beyond a reasonable doubt. They go on to indicate: "The fact that there was no killing at Sivci could suggest that the killing of villagers was not a planned part of this particular episode of ethnic cleansing of the two villages, in which the accused took part; it is accordingly a distinct possibility that it may have been the act of a quite distinct group of armed men, or the unauthorised and unforeseen act of one of the force that entered Sivci ..." We suggest to you that by use of terms such as "bare possibility" and "could suggest," the Trial Chamber is indicating its misapplication of proof beyond reasonable doubt. Neither of these two bases for the Trial Chamber's decision is reasonably supported by the facts that they found in this case. In this regard, Your Honours, we suggest to you that, though the issue is different than this morning, the same test would still be applied by Your Honours in resolving this issue. That would be, in looking at the facts that were found by the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber will have erred if there is no reasonable support for their decision, if no reasonable person could have concluded as they did, and we suggest that is the case here, even taking into account the deference that you give to decisions on fact of a Trial Chamber. If we could look just for a moment at some of the facts that the Trial Chamber found in this case, we believe it puts our position in very strong perspective. At paragraph 369 of its findings of fact, the Trial Chamber found among the following: "... witnesses did indeed see the accused in Sivci and Jaskici on 14 June 1992, that he entered those two villages together with other armed men as alleged in paragraph 12 of the Indictment, and in Sivci took part in the removal of separated men from that village ... and in Jazkici took part in the calling-out of residents and the separation of men from women and children." The Trial Chamber was further satisfied that: "... said group were forcibly removed from the village of Jazkici ..." a listed number of men, "and that the accused participated in their removal and further that the accused beat ..." and then the Trial Chamber lists a number of men that they were convinced the accused beat in the village of Jaskici. The Trial Chamber indicated that: "Of the killing of the five men in Jaskici, the witnesses ... saw their five dead bodies lying in the village when the women were able to leave their houses after the armed men had gone ... That the armed men were violent is not in doubt." That was found by the Trial Chamber. "... a number of these witnesses were themselves threatened with death by the armed men as the men of the village were being taken away. Apart from that, their beating of the men from the village ... is further evidence of their violence." In paragraph 371, the Trial Chamber found: "The group of armed men were relatively few in number and the accused was one of them and took an active part in the rounding up of the men in the village ..." In paragraph 372, the Trial Chamber found: "The village of Jaskici had been quiet before the armed men came; they arrived to the sound of gunfire, conducted with the threats of death and great violence a search of the village ... brutally beat the village men as they lay on the road and, when they left taking the village men with them, shots were heard and five dead men remained lying where they had been killed in the village." In regard to these five dead men and where they were lying, during the trial, there was undisputed testimony of witnesses that out of the list of five men who were killed, two of those victims at least, the bodies of two of those victims were found on the road not far from where the accused and the other members of his armed group had beaten them and in the direction in which the accused and the other armed men had taken the village men away from the village. We suggest to you, Your Honours, that given the facts that were found by the Trial Chamber, they could not have reasonably concluded that the accused had no liability for these murders. If we would look a moment at liability and the findings that the Trial Chamber made concerning liability, at paragraph 764 of the judgement, they found that under the Statute, Article 7(1), that for liability to be attributed, "we must first find intent, and intent is an awareness of the act of participation and a conscious decision to participate in the commission of the crimes." They also indicated that intent can be inferred from all the facts in the circumstances of a case. They also found the second requirement for liability as a participant was participation in conduct that contributed to the commission of an illegal act and that this conduct must have been deliberate and directly and substantially affected the commission of that crime. They also found at paragraph 678 to 687 that: "An accused need not have intended or known of all of the consequences of an act but that an accused who participates directly, deliberately, and substantially with the requisite intent will be responsible for all the natural results that flow from his acts." They gave as an example that the presence for one beating, "if an accused is present for one beating and then stays with the group as they go on to beat another, then that presence, that remaining presence has an encouraging effect and would make an accused criminally liable as a participant." In paragraph 685, they also talked about this idea of a common purpose or a common criminal enterprise, and they indicated that people altogether at the same time taking part in a common criminal enterprise, each in his own way assisting the other, these people are guilty. Now, taking those ideas of liability in the context of these facts, we suggest to you that, indeed, it was not a reasonable conclusion for the Trial Chamber to determine that this accused was not guilty. If we look, first of all, at their conclusion that others may have committed this crime, others than the accused and his group in Jaskici, the facts simply do not support that in any reasonable way. We had evidence at the trial that during the time that men were taken out and put on the street and beaten, women in houses were able to look out the window and observe these beatings. None of these women indicated that new people arrived to participate in these acts. We also had evidence at trial to indicate that as the accused and his armed group led men away from the village, women were able to watch that happen. There was no indication that anyone saw another group come and join with the group of the accused. There was indication, there was evidence at this trial that this group that came to Jaskici was a very violent group, that they were engaged in very violent behaviours, that they threatened to kill members of the village if they did not do as they were told. So the threat of death hung in the air in Jaskici. The Trial Chamber found no such killings in Sivci. There is a distinction here. The evidence relating to Sivci showed the accused involved in one minor part of what happened in Sivci. When we come to Jaskici, the accused is an integral part of the violence in that village, and when he and this small group of men move away from Sivci and come into their own in Jaskici, we see an escalation of the violence and the very threat of death in the air. The facts support the kind of circumstances where death is a very natural consequence of the crimes that this group were conducting in this village. It certainly cannot be said that this would be an unforeseen consequence of the extreme violence that was visited upon the members of this village. Secondly, if we look at the evidence as to what happened in Jaskici and this accused, he was certainly aware of his participation. He certainly made a conscious decision to participate. His activities were deliberate. They substantially contributed to the crimes that were taking place there. Then we come down to, what about the killings? Were the killings intended? Were they a natural consequence of what was going on? We suggest that if they were not intended in the sense of as the group came into the village, they had a conscious desire to kill, then they were a natural consequence of what occurred in that village and that all of those armed members in that village were willing to engage in such conduct. We know that because they threatened the villagers with death, and that included the accused who threatened one of the villagers with death. We have intent, we have participation, and now in Jaskici itself with this small group of men, we have participation in a common criminal enterprise. This common criminal enterprise was not an unforeseen or an unauthorised enterprise because the enterprise in Jaskici was the same as the enterprise in Sivci was the same as the enterprise throughout all of opstina Prijedor, and that enterprise was to rid opstina Prijedor of non-Serbs, to rid them of all or at least most of the non-Serbs in that area and to do it by a variety of means, including killings. Because throughout the evidence in Tadic, you find situations where villages were cleansed, people were killed. Non-Serbs were taken to camps; they were killed. So to cleanse the area included killings and other violent forms of conduct, as well as less violent but certainly coercive means of removing non-Serbs from the opstina. It was not an unforeseen act in the context of this ethnic cleansing. It was not an unauthorised act. It went on and on and on. It was part of a plan. There was a common criminal enterprise, and the Trial Chamber, when it evaluated that common criminal enterprise, erred by restricting it to too small of an area. It should have taken into account the common criminal enterprise that existed throughout opstina Prijedor and, we would suggest, existed throughout the entire area where Serbs attempted to ethnically cleanse non-Serbs. If we take this context then, we suggest to you that the Trial Chamber erred not because we would substitute a separate reasoned judgement but because there's no reasonable basis for their judgement. Their two bases to find the accused not guilty are not reasonably supported by the record or by the law, not supported by the facts they themselves found. If we were to assume that, indeed, a component or one person from this larger force that entered Sivci was the person who came to Jaskici and killed these five men, were we to assume that, even though we suggest to you it is incredible, the accused would nonetheless be guilty because he participated with that armed force in Sivci. He participated in Jaskici with the same common criminal purpose, to rid these villages and the opstina of non-Serbs and to do it with violence or with less coercive measures if possible. Killing was not something that he could not have foreseen. He himself was involved in killings and not just the killings that are contested here, but you have counts involving Sefik Sivac and counts involving Salih Elezovic in the Omarska camp where the Trial Chamber found that these men were beaten, the accused participated to some extent in those beatings, and the Trial Chamber found that, as a result of those beatings, those men died. The evidence against this accused is an evidence of extreme violence and brutal treatment. It could not have been unforeseen to him that this would have happened; it certainly was not unauthorised that it would happened. By not taking into account all of these facts that they themselves found, we suggest that the Trial Chamber erred in arriving at its decision that there was a failure of proof beyond reasonable doubt. One last point on this issue: The Prosecution suggests that it is incredible to say someone came from outside this armed group and committed these crimes. Why do we say that? Earlier, I pointed out that no one in the village who was able to look out at what was happening saw anyone come into the village and join this group. No one heard anyone come into this village and join this group. No one heard the accused's group leave, a period of silence, and then another group come in and shots being fired. All of what happened was in the context of the accused and his armed group in this village. So in order to assume that someone else committed this crime, you would have to assume one of two things: First, that these other participants came into the village were totally stealthy about their approach, made no noise, did not come accompanied by gunfire as the accused had, made no words of greeting to this group in the village; simply came stealthily to the group, blended in with them, and immediately killed five men. We suggest that that is implausible. The second possibility would be that this group came in, it came in accompanied by gunfire as the accused had, it spoke to the accused's group, it mingled in with this group, and then it committed these killings, but the women in the houses, who had the opportunity to hear what was going on and to occasionally see what was going on, never saw that and never heard that, and we suggest on these facts that is not a plausible theory either. So for these reasons, we suggest that the Trial Chamber did err in this regard, and we would ask you to reverse those findings of not guilty as to the killings of the five men in the village of Jaskici. Turning to ground number 5, and before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, I understand you to mean that the error which you say was committed by the Trial Chamber was twofold, that in determining the content of the idea of common purpose or common enterprise in this case, they should have taken into account, but did not, the fact that the accused was engaged in implementing a general policy of ethnic cleansing, the characteristics of which should have been known to him and which implied the possibility of violence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. In fact, the natural consequence would include violence to include murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And your second point is, as I understand you, the Trial Chamber expressed a doubt based on the possibility, as it saw it, of elements from a larger group coming into the locality and committing the deed. I understand you to say that there is no material on the record to support that possibility and that a doubt must always have some factual foundation for the doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could perhaps put that slightly differently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please pass to your next point then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could respond to your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber, based on a bare possibility, concluded that another group may have been involved or another individual may have actually carried out the killings. Our position is that the bare possibility of something does not rise to the level of reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Speculative.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is speculative. And that reasonable doubt has to be a fair and rational doubt based on assessment of the evidence, and that on the assessment of this evidence, there is no evidence from which one could reasonably conclude that persons from outside came to Jaskici and committed the murders. Secondly, if you were to determine one could reasonably conclude it was part of this larger force, the accused would still be liable under the common criminal enterprise doctrine because of this wider ethnic cleansing that all of them were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We are ready to hear you on the last point.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Ground 5 of the Prosecution's submission is one of the grounds, Your Honour, that you requested we address in that it deals with the Trial Chamber's denial of the Prosecution request that the Defence be ordered to disclose statements of witnesses they were going to call or had called in their case at trial. This ground of appeal does not meet the requirements of Article 25. We are not suggesting that this decision by the Trial Chamber invalidated the judgement. We have no basis to argue that this decision resulted in a miscarriage of justice. We request that the Appeals Chamber consider this issue because we believe it is an issue of significance to all practitioners before this Tribunal and to Trial Chambers before this Tribunal, and we believe that as it stands now, there is persuasive authority from this case that the Defence may not be ordered to disclose such witness statements. Our position is that is an erroneous authority, that indeed a Trial Chamber has the authority to order such disclosure, that such an order would not violate any of the statutory provisions or Rules of this Tribunal, that such an order would not violate any fundamental rights of the accused, and that indeed such an order would contribute to the overall mandate of this Tribunal, and that is, for the factfinders to be given evidence which has been fully tested. One of the ways to test that evidence is for witnesses who have made statements that may be considered inconsistent, to be confronted with those statements and to be allowed to explain those inconsistencies. Inconsistencies may or may not have a bearing on the weight to be given evidence, but the factfinder should have the benefit of weighing such inconsistencies in arriving at their determination. We suggest that the Trial Chamber erred in determining that a privilege would be applied which does not exist before this Tribunal. The Judges in this Tribunal had the opportunity to enact rules that would incorporate the privileges the Judges believed were necessary to ensure a fair trial and proper functioning of the Tribunal. The Judges of this Tribunal chose not to set forth the privilege that was used in this case. We suggest that privilege should not be incorporated into the Rules of the Tribunal or into the law of the Tribunal. When we are looking at privileges, we suggest that we must be very, very careful in applying them because a privilege inevitably will result in what could be highly credible evidence, highly relevant evidence, not being presented to the factfinder. So there must be some compelling reason to have a privilege that excludes relevant evidence or relevant inquiry. This Tribunal did not adopt the privilege that was used here, it adopted a very narrow attorney-client privilege. It did not go beyond that to include that statements given to Defence counsel were privileged, not, at least, where these witnesses then come forward to testify. It could be argued by some that to grant the Prosecution's ground of appeal here would infringe the accused's right not to present a defence. We suggest that, on further reflection, that is not an appropriate argument because when this provision will come into play is when the Defence has chosen to put on a defence, they have chosen to present evidence, so it in no way compels them to present evidence, but it says, once they have chosen to do so, that evidence should be subjected to the same scrutiny that the evidence presented by the Prosecution should be subjected to. Why is that? Is it to give the Prosecution an edge in the case? No. It is for the same reason that Prosecution evidence should be subjected to scrutiny: So that the factfinder, in determining what are the reliable facts, has the benefit of testing of that evidence, very rigorous testing of that evidence. One of the ways, traditionally, such evidence is tested, is to look at prior statements that may have inconsistencies and to determine the relevance, if any, of those inconsistencies when assessing credibility. The Trial Chamber, we suggest, also erred when it determined that it would not look beyond common law jurisdictions and practice in resolving this issue. This Tribunal, in many ways, has a wondrous and unique opportunity. It is an international tribunal that blends the law from all the civilised societies of the world. It takes the inquisitorial system, it takes the common law system, it takes variance within all those systems, and the unique opportunity is to take all of those systems and from them to choose the very best assets so that this Tribunal can come up with procedures and rules that best enable you to do what you are mandated to do: within the protections given to the accused, to determine the truthfulness of what happened, a truth-seeking process. That is what criminal justice systems always are. But here you can blend all aspects and come up with what is best, and we suggest that what is best is to subject the Defence evidence to the same level of scrutiny as the Prosecution evidence by way of examination of prior statements.
