That is what best gives the factfinder the ability to determine what is the truth. Now, there may be some issue that would arise as to what is a statement, and that would be an issue that would have to be resolved. Would notes of a Defence counsel be a statement? We have the same issue with notes that are taken by investigators. That issue can be resolved by Trial Chambers. But what we would ask this Appellate Chamber to do would be to find that there is no privilege such as the Trial Chamber set forth, and that when the Defence determines that the accused will put on evidence, that at some point, either before the witness is called or after the witness is called and before cross-examination, the Prosecution has the right to receive any statements that that witness may have made to the Defence or that may be in the possession of the Defence. If the Defence is concerned that this may cause some witnesses to be hesitant to come forward, we would ask: What is the basis of the concern? If it is because the witness is going to change their story, the Trial Chamber should know that. If it is because there is sensitive information that the witness does not want to come forward, the Defence always has the possibility of submitting such statements to the Trial Chamber for an in-camera review. So that should not be dispositive of the issue. So we suggest for policy reasons and because it violates no fundamental right of the accused and because it is not inconsistent with the Statute and our Rules, that this Appellate Chamber find that the Trial Chamber erred and find that the Trial Chamber does have the power to order production of such statements and should do so in the circumstances that I have described. I have no further comments on that ground. If there are any questions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You suggested an idea, say you are right, that there are legal systems, the practice wherein is consistent with the position you are taking; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Such as what? Continental systems?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: For example, Your Honour, I believe in practice in a continental system you would have that because witnesses who appear to give evidence for the Defence, if there were statements, those statements would be part of a dossier both parties would have access to. So in that sense, certainly the Prosecution would have access to evidence that could be relevant for the Defence. In the United States, Your Honour, I will speak for just a moment, if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- of the jurisdiction from which I come, which is the military system in the United States, and the military system, for many, many years, had very, very broad disclosure obligations by the Prosecution to the Defence and in recent years has expanded the disclosure obligations of the Defence to the Prosecution, including providing witness statements, and the theory is that it will enhance the truth-seeking process and it does not violate a right of the accused, once the accused decides to put on evidence, for them to disclose statements of their witnesses so that the factfinder may be more informed about any potential inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are inviting the Appeals Chamber to take the position that the only privileges which the accused has are privileges set forth either in the Statute or in the Rules?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, unless, of course, in the Statute and Rules the provisions of either the Articles or the Rules would be in direct contradiction to a well-established and universally-accepted principle of the fundamental right of the accused. For example, if the Statute were to say that the accused had to present evidence and prove his innocence, then, of course, we would not support that. But we don't see any such extreme measure. So, yes, with that sort of extreme situation aside, that is what we are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How would you react to a possible argument that the Rules being subordinate to the Statute, the imperative direction of the Statute that the accused should be afforded a fair trial, overrides the Rules and means that in a possible case, although the Rules do not provide for it, the Trial Chamber was competent to exclude material on the ground that to admit the material might be unfair to the accused? I am not putting that proposition to you as mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do agree that the Statute overrides the Rules and I do agree that if a Trial Chamber were to find that it could not enforce a Rule because it would deprive the accused of a fair trial, then the statutory provision for a fair trial would have to prevail. I think there would have to be a showing of the deprival of a fair trial, however. It is interesting to note, if we talk about the Statute and we look at the Statute, we have been discussing, earlier today in much detail and yesterday as well, Article 21 of the Statute, which, of course, speaks in terms of the accused's rights at trial, and it indicates, if we look at paragraph 4: "4. In the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees, in full equality ..." Interestingly, if we look at sub-part (e): "(e) to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him." Well, one of the conditions for witnesses against him is that if we have statements of those witnesses, they're turned over to the Defence. So if we are talking about full equality, that would say that the Defence turns their statements over to the Prosecution because that is certainly a condition the Prosecution must meet to call witnesses. We are not saying that we have to create statements, but if we have them, we have to turn them over. So, yes, Statute would prevail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have to turn them over --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, by the Statute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- pursuant to a direction issuing from the Rules; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, Rule 66 is one and also, of course, Rule 68 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there a similar requirement in relation to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, there is not, and that was litigated at trial, that there is nothing that says the Defence does not have to in the Rules but there is nothing that specifically requires production, although I think in the current Rules, which would not be applicable to this case, but in the current Rules, at least the Defence has to give a summary of the facts to which witnesses will testify. So we are at least moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any questions? Ms. Hollis, we are obliged to you and to your colleague for your assistance. Does that conclude your arguments?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then on the scheme, at 17.30, which is creeping up on us, we would be hearing next Mr. Clegg, and I take it you would readily concur with the Bench that it would meet your convenience to start in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then the court stands adjourned until 10.00 tomorrow.
